solutions.reliable: The full jar holds 20 and 13 are already in it, so 20 - 13 = 7 more fit. Check: 13 + 7 = 20. The idea to keep: whole minus the part you have gives the part that is missing.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding a missing part from the whole is the core bar model, and counting the starting number is a common slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Cat has 4 marbles. Ben has 2 more marbles than Cat. Ann has 5 more marbles than Ben. How many marbles does Ann have?

choices.misconception: I found how many marbles Ben has and stopped there.
I added the 2 and the 5 and forgot to start from Cat's 4.
I added 5 to Cat's 4 and skipped the step through Ben.
I added up the marbles of all three children.

hints: Start with the child whose number you know.
Draw three bars. Cat's is known. Ben's bar is Cat's bar plus a piece, and Ann's bar is Ben's bar plus a bigger piece. Go one child at a time.
Ben has 4 + 2 = 6 marbles. Ann has 5 more than Ben, so add 5 to 6.

solutions.reliable: Cat has 4. Ben has 2 more than Cat, so 6. Ann has 5 more than Ben, so 6 + 5 = 11. The idea to keep: when each person is compared with the next, follow the chain one step at a time from the person you know.
solutions.elegant: Ann has 5 more than Ben, who has 2 more than Cat, so Ann has 2 + 5 = 7 more than Cat: 4 + 7 = 11. The idea to keep: differences along a chain add up.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparison chains reward working one step at a time, and skipping the middle person is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Kim's tower has 3 times as many blocks as Ben's tower. Kim's tower has 10 more blocks than Ben's. How many blocks are in Ben's tower?

choices.misconception: I took the 3 away from the 10 instead of drawing the towers.
I thought Ben's tower had as many blocks as the difference.
I found how many blocks are in Kim's tower instead of Ben's.
I multiplied the 10 extra blocks by 3 instead of sharing them.

hints: Draw Ben's tower as one box.
Kim's tower is three of Ben's boxes. Line the two bars up: the part of Kim's bar that sticks out past Ben's is the 10 extra blocks. Count how many boxes that is.
Kim has 3 boxes and Ben has 1, so the extra part is 2 boxes. Those 2 boxes hold 10 blocks.

solutions.reliable: Draw Ben's tower as one box and Kim's as three boxes of the same size. Kim's bar sticks out by 2 boxes, and that extra part is 10 blocks, so one box is 5. Ben has 5 blocks and Kim has 15. Check: 15 is 3 times 5 and 15 - 5 = 10. The idea to keep: in a times-as-many question, the difference is a whole number of boxes, so find what one box holds.
solutions.elegant: Try the choices: if Ben has 5, Kim has 15, and 15 is 10 more than 5. No other choice works both ways. The idea to keep: a choice can be checked against every fact in the question.

problems.whyOnTest: It needs an idea, not a sum: the extra blocks are exactly two of Ben's boxes, which a bar model shows at once.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What number is made of 4 tens and 12 ones?

choices.misconception: I added 4 and 12 as if they were all ones.
I wrote the 4 tens and kept only the 2 from the 12 ones.
I treated the 12 as tens too, so I had 16 tens.
I wrote the 4 and then the 12 next to each other.

hints: Can 12 ones all fit in the ones place?
Ten ones make one ten. Turn as many of the 12 ones as you can into a ten, then count the tens and the ones that are left.
12 ones are 1 ten and 2 ones. Add that ten to the 4 tens you already have.

solutions.reliable: 4 tens are 40 and 12 ones are 12, so the number is 40 + 12 = 52. Another way: 12 ones are 1 ten and 2 ones, so there are 5 tens and 2 ones, which is 52. The idea to keep: ten ones always make one more ten.

problems.whyOnTest: Place value means knowing that ten ones make a ten, and a number with more than 9 ones checks that a student regroups instead of writing digits side by side.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A number is between 40 and 50. Its two digits add up to 10. What is the number?

choices.misconception: I found the ones digit, 6, and gave that instead of the whole number.
I added 10 to 40 instead of making the digits add up to 10.
I found digits that add up to 10 but did not check the number is between 40 and 50.
I put the 6 in the tens place and the 4 in the ones place.

hints: What must the tens digit be?
Every number between 40 and 50 has the same tens digit. Use that to work out what the ones digit must be so that the two digits add up to 10.
The tens digit is 4, so the ones digit must be 10 take away 4.

solutions.reliable: Numbers between 40 and 50 all have tens digit 4. The digits add up to 10, so the ones digit is 10 - 4 = 6. The number is 46. Check: it is between 40 and 50 and 4 + 6 = 10. The idea to keep: use the clue that fixes one digit first, then find the other.

problems.whyOnTest: Digit clues test place value: the tens digit is fixed by where the number sits, and the trap is swapping the digits.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Every dart on a board scores 1, 3, 5 or 7 points. Lea throws three darts and all of them hit the board. Which total could she score?

choices.misconception: I used 3 + 3 = 6 and forgot that Lea throws a third dart.
I used 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 without checking which scores are on the board.
I used 5 + 5 = 10, which is only two darts.
I used 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 without checking which scores are on the board.

hints: Are the scores on the board odd or even?
Every score on the board is odd. Think about what happens to odd and even when you add two odd numbers, and then add one more odd number.
Odd + odd is even, and even + odd is odd. So three odd scores always add to an odd total. Which choice is odd, and can you make it?

solutions.reliable: Every score is odd. Two odd numbers add to an even number, and adding a third odd number makes the total odd again. So three darts always give an odd total. Only 13 is odd, and 7 + 5 + 1 = 13 shows it can really happen. The idea to keep: add odd numbers in pairs, since each pair is even, and one left over makes the total odd.
solutions.elegant: Each odd score is an even number plus 1. Three darts give three of those extra 1s, which is 3, and 3 is odd, so the total is odd. Then check 13 = 7 + 5 + 1. The idea to keep: count the leftover 1s to decide odd or even.

problems.whyOnTest: Parity lets a student rule out four choices without trying a single sum, and still check that the last one really works.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mo had 16 grapes. He ate half of them. Then he gave half of the grapes he had left to his sister. How many grapes does Mo have now?

choices.misconception: I thought half and then half again meant all the grapes were gone.
I halved one time too many and went from 4 down to 2.
I stopped after he ate half and forgot about his sister.
I only took away the grapes he gave his sister and forgot the ones he ate.

hints: The second half is half of what is left, not half of 16.
Do the two steps one at a time. After each step, write down how many grapes Mo still has, and take the next half of that new number.
Half of 16 is 8, so 8 are left after eating. Now find half of 8 and take it away.

solutions.reliable: Mo eats half of 16, which is 8, so 8 are left. He gives half of those 8, which is 4, to his sister, so 8 - 4 = 4 are left. The idea to keep: a fraction of what is left changes size at each step, so work one step at a time.

problems.whyOnTest: Taking a fraction of what is left, rather than of the start, is a classic two-step trap with fractions of a quantity.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which number is 3 less than 51?

choices.misconception: I took 3 away from the tens digit instead of from the whole number.
I counted back one step too many.
I counted 51, 50, 49 and counted 51 as one of the three steps.
I added 3 instead of taking 3 away.

hints: Count back one step at a time.
Picture 51 on a number line and take three steps to the left. Only the steps count, not the number you start on. Be careful as you go back past 50.
One step back from 51 is 50, two steps back is 49. Take one more step.

solutions.reliable: Start at 51 and step back three times: 50, 49, 48. So 3 less than 51 is 48. Check: 48 + 3 = 51. The idea to keep: on a number line count the jumps, not the number you start on.
solutions.elegant: Take 1 to reach 50, then 2 more to reach 48. The idea to keep: break a jump at a round number.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting back across a ten is where off-by-one slips happen, and the number line keeps the steps honest.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tim is 8 years old. His sister is 3 years younger than Tim. How old was his sister 2 years ago?

choices.misconception: I found how old his sister is now and stopped there.
I found how old Tim was 2 years ago instead of his sister.
I added 2 years instead of going back 2 years.
I made his sister 3 years older than Tim instead of younger, then went back 2 years.

hints: Who does the question ask about, and when?
Underline what the question wants: the sister, and her age in the past. First find her age now, then go back in time.
His sister is 8 - 3 = 5 now. Two years ago she was 2 years younger than that.

solutions.reliable: Tim is 8 and his sister is 3 years younger, so she is 5 now. Two years ago she was 5 - 2 = 3. The idea to keep: before answering, check who and when the question asks about.

problems.whyOnTest: Age questions ask about a particular person at a particular time, and most wrong answers answer a different person or time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Bea has 7 stickers. Cal has 3 more stickers than Bea. How many stickers do Bea and Cal have together?

choices.misconception: I found the difference between 7 and 3 instead of Cal's number.
I found how many stickers Cal has and forgot to add Bea's.
I added 7 and 3 and then added the 3 extra again instead of adding Bea's 7.
I gave Cal the same number as Bea and added 7 and 7.

hints: The question asks about both children.
There are two steps. First find Cal's number from what the question says about him, then answer the real question, which is about the two children together.
Cal has 7 + 3 = 10 stickers. Now add Bea's 7 to Cal's 10.

solutions.reliable: Cal has 3 more than Bea, so Cal has 7 + 3 = 10. Together they have 7 + 10 = 17. The idea to keep: finding one person's number is often only a step, so check what the last sentence actually asks for.
solutions.elegant: Together is two of Bea's amount plus Cal's extra 3: 7 + 7 + 3 = 17. The idea to keep: picture the two bars as equal parts plus an extra piece.

problems.whyOnTest: Stopping after the first step is the most common contest slip, and this question has a choice waiting for it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two paper strips are each 10 cm long. They are glued together so that they overlap by 3 cm, making one long strip. How long is the long strip?

choices.misconception: I took the 3 cm overlap away from one strip and stopped there.
I took the 3 cm overlap away from both strips, so I got 7 + 7.
I put the strips end to end and forgot that they overlap.
I added the 3 cm overlap on instead of taking it away.

hints: Draw the two strips, one a little on top of the other.
The 3 cm where the strips overlap belongs to both strips, but it is only 3 cm of the long strip. How far does the second strip stick out past the end of the first?
The first strip gives 10 cm. The second strip sticks out past it by 10 - 3 = 7 cm.

solutions.reliable: Draw the first strip, 10 cm long. The second strip starts 3 cm before the end of the first, so only 10 - 3 = 7 cm of it sticks out past the first strip. The long strip is 10 + 7 = 17 cm. The idea to keep: a quick drawing shows that an overlap is counted once, not twice.
solutions.elegant: End to end the strips would make 10 + 10 = 20 cm. The overlap hides 3 cm of that, so the long strip is 20 - 3 = 17 cm. The idea to keep: count everything, then take away the part that is counted twice.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the diagram makes the overlap visible, and each wrong choice comes from taking the overlap away the wrong number of times.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a straight road, the school is 5 blocks from Pia's house, and the park is 2 blocks from the school. How far from Pia's house could the park be?

choices.misconception: I put the park between the house and the school and forgot it could be past the school.
I put the park past the school and forgot it could be back toward the house.
I gave the two distances in the question instead of the distance from the house to the park.
I multiplied 5 by 2 instead of putting the places on the road.

hints: Draw the road. Where can the park go?
Draw the house and the school on a line. The park is 2 blocks from the school, and there are two places on a straight road that are 2 blocks from the school. Check both.
If the park is on the house side of the school, it is 5 - 2 blocks from the house. If it is on the far side, it is 5 + 2 blocks from the house.

solutions.reliable: Put the house at 0 and the school at 5 on a number line. The park is 2 blocks from the school, so it is at 3 or at 7. That makes it 3 blocks or 7 blocks from the house, and both can happen. The idea to keep: when a drawing can be made more than one way, draw every way before you answer.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the diagram reveals a second case that is easy to miss when you only picture one arrangement.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square garden has sides of 5 m. Fence posts stand all the way round it: one at every corner and one every 1 m along each side. How many posts are there?

choices.misconception: I counted only the posts between the corners and left out the corner posts.
I added one extra post to finish, as you would on a straight fence.
I counted 6 posts on each side, so every corner post was counted twice.
I counted the 1 m squares that fill the garden instead of the posts round it.

hints: How far is it all the way round?
Walk once round the garden. Every 1 m you reach a new post, and when you get back to the start you are at the first post again, so it is not a new one.
The distance round is 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 m, and there is one post for each metre you walk.

solutions.reliable: The distance all the way round is 4 x 5 = 20 m. Walking round, there is a post at every metre mark, and the last metre brings you back to the first post. So there are 20 posts. The idea to keep: on a closed loop, the number of posts equals the number of gaps.
solutions.elegant: Each side has its 5 posts if you count the corner where it starts but not the corner where it ends. 4 sides give 4 x 5 = 20 posts, with every corner counted exactly once. The idea to keep: give each shared corner to just one side.

problems.whyOnTest: It joins perimeter with the fence-post idea, and the closed loop is what makes the usual plus-one wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square has sides of 4 cm. A rectangle 6 cm long has the same distance all the way round as the square. How wide is the rectangle?

choices.misconception: I gave the side of the square instead of working out the rectangle.
I took one long side away from the distance round and halved what was left, forgetting the other long side.
I halved the distance round and stopped, which gives the length and width added together.
I took one long side away from the distance round and stopped there.

hints: First find the distance round the square.
The square's four sides give the distance round. The rectangle has the same total. Take away its two long sides, and what is left is shared by its two short sides.
The distance round is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm. The two long sides of the rectangle use 6 + 6 = 12 cm of that.

solutions.reliable: The square's distance round is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm. The rectangle's two long sides make 6 + 6 = 12 cm, so its two short sides make 16 - 12 = 4 cm, and each one is 2 cm. Check: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16. The idea to keep: a rectangle has two of each side, so take both long sides away before sharing what is left.
solutions.elegant: Half of the distance round is one length plus one width. Half of 16 is 8, and 8 - 6 = 2 cm. The idea to keep: half the perimeter of a rectangle is length plus width.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards from a perimeter needs the idea that each side comes twice, and every wrong choice forgets that somewhere.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Mia writes a word in capital letters and holds it up to a mirror. Which word looks exactly the same in the mirror?

choices.misconception: I checked that M, A and T each look the same in a mirror, but forgot that the mirror also swaps their order, so it shows TAM.
I saw that BOB reads the same backwards, but forgot that the mirror also turns each B the wrong way round.
I checked that each letter of BOX can be folded top to bottom, but a mirror held in front of a word flips it left to right.
I knew S looks the same when it is turned upside down, so I thought it also looks the same in a mirror.

hints: Check two things: each letter, and the order of the letters.
A mirror swaps left and right. So every letter must look the same when flipped left to right, and the word must also read the same backwards. Test each word for both.
MAT turns into TAM. In BOB, BOX and SOS, the letters B and S face the wrong way. Now check the last word.

solutions.reliable: A mirror swaps left and right. That changes a word in two ways: each letter is flipped, and the order of the letters is reversed. MAT shows as TAM. In BOB, BOX and SOS, every B or S comes out facing the wrong way. In TOOT, the letters T and O look the same when flipped, and TOOT reads the same backwards, so the mirror shows TOOT. The idea to keep: a mirror flips the whole picture, so check the letters and their order.

problems.whyOnTest: A mirror tests two kinds of matching at once: each letter must match its flip, and the word must read the same backwards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A capital letter is written on a card. Ana turns the card halfway round, flat on the table, so the top is at the bottom. Which letter looks exactly the same?

choices.misconception: I checked that A matches when folded down the middle and thought that meant it looks the same after a half turn.
I flipped the E over from top to bottom, like a mirror, instead of spinning it round.
I pictured M turned round and thought it was still an M.
I thought a V turned round is still a V.

hints: Try writing each letter on a scrap of paper and turning the paper round.
A half turn spins the letter round its middle, so the top goes to the bottom and the left goes to the right at the same time. This is not the same as folding or flipping it.
Spin each letter in your head. M becomes a W and V becomes an upside-down V. Look at N.

solutions.reliable: Spinning by a half turn moves the top to the bottom and the left to the right. A, M and V end up pointing the other way, and E ends up facing backwards. N spun round is still N. The idea to keep: a half turn is not a fold, so a letter can match one and not the other.

problems.whyOnTest: Students often mix up folding symmetry with turning symmetry, and this question separates the two.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ella makes a flag with 3 stripes, one above another. Each stripe is red or blue. The top and bottom stripes must be the same colour. How many different flags can she make?

choices.misconception: I only counted the flags that are all one colour.
I listed red-red-red, red-blue-red and blue-blue-blue and missed blue-red-blue.
I counted the flags that use both colours instead of the flags that follow the rule.
I counted every flag with 3 stripes and forgot the rule about the top and bottom.

hints: Start with the top stripe: red or blue?
Draw a tree. The top stripe has two choices. The middle stripe then has two choices. The bottom stripe has no choice at all, because the rule decides it.
Top red: the middle is red or blue, and the bottom must be red. Top blue: the same again.

solutions.reliable: Draw a tree. If the top is red, the middle can be red or blue and the bottom must be red: red-red-red and red-blue-red. If the top is blue, the same gives blue-blue-blue and blue-red-blue. That is 4 flags. The idea to keep: a rule can take away a branch completely, so only branch where there is a real choice.
solutions.elegant: Only the top and middle stripes are free choices, 2 each, and the bottom copies the top. So 2 x 2 = 4. The idea to keep: count only the choices that are really free.

problems.whyOnTest: A tree diagram with a rule teaches that some steps have no choice at all, which separates careful counters from guessers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: There are 3 paths between Ian's house and the park. Ian walks to the park on one path and comes home on a different path. How many different trips can he make?

choices.misconception: I only counted the paths left for the way home.
I only counted the ways to get to the park.
I added the 3 ways there and the 2 ways back instead of matching them up.
I let Ian come home on the same path he took to the park.

hints: Call the paths 1, 2 and 3.
Draw a tree. The first branches are the paths to the park. From each, draw branches only for the paths he is allowed to take home, then count the branch ends.
If he goes on path 1, he can come home on path 2 or path 3. The same happens for each path there.

solutions.reliable: Name the paths 1, 2 and 3. Going on path 1, he can come home on 2 or 3. Going on path 2, he can come home on 1 or 3. Going on path 3, he can come home on 1 or 2. That is 6 trips. The idea to keep: draw the tree and remove the branches the rule does not allow.
solutions.elegant: There are 3 ways there and, because the path home must be different, 2 ways back for each. So 3 x 2 = 6 trips. The idea to keep: a restriction can make the second choice smaller than the first.

problems.whyOnTest: It adds a simple rule to a tree diagram, and the wrong answers come from ignoring the rule or from adding instead of branching.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The word TIGER is written again and again with no gaps: TIGERTIGERTIGER and so on. What is the 18th letter?

choices.misconception: I found that letter 15 ends a word and gave the first letter of the next word, which is letter 16.
I counted one letter too few and gave the 17th letter.
I counted one letter too many and gave the 19th letter.
I found that the third TIGER ends at letter 15 and gave that letter instead of counting on.

hints: Each TIGER uses the same number of letters.
The pattern repeats every 5 letters. Jump ahead a whole word at a time until you are close to 18, then count the last few letters one by one.
Three whole words use 15 letters, so letter 15 is an R. Count on 3 more letters from the start of the next TIGER.

solutions.reliable: TIGER has 5 letters, so the words end at letters 5, 10 and 15. Letter 16 is T, letter 17 is I and letter 18 is G. The idea to keep: in a repeating pattern, jump by whole repeats, then count only the leftover steps.
solutions.elegant: Counting in fives, 18 is 3 more than 15, so the 18th letter is the 3rd letter of TIGER, which is G. The idea to keep: the leftover after the last full repeat tells you the position in the pattern.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding a far-away place in a repeating pattern rewards jumping by whole repeats instead of counting every letter.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tile squares grow: 1 tile, then 2 rows of 2, then 3 rows of 3, and so on. How many tiles are added to go from the 4th square to the 5th?

choices.misconception: I added just one new row of 5 tiles.
I added a new row of 5 and a new column of 5, and counted the corner tile twice.
I gave how many tiles are in the 4th square.
I gave how many tiles are in the 5th square instead of how many are added.

hints: Draw the 4th square, then make it one bigger.
To grow a square by one, you add a new row along the bottom and a new column down the side. Be careful with the tile in the corner where they meet.
The 4th square has 4 rows of 4. Add a column of 4 down the side and a row of 5 along the bottom.

solutions.reliable: The 4th square is 4 rows of 4 tiles, which is 16 tiles. The 5th square is 5 rows of 5 tiles, which is 25 tiles. So 25 - 16 = 9 tiles are added. Check by drawing: a column of 4 down the side and a row of 5 along the bottom is 4 + 5 = 9. The idea to keep: growing a square adds an L shape, so count its corner once.
solutions.elegant: The new tiles form an L: one arm of 4 and one arm of 5, so 4 + 5 = 9. The idea to keep: each step adds the old side plus the new side.

problems.whyOnTest: Growing square patterns need the picture, not just the numbers, and the corner tile counted twice is the classic slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, 20 is exactly halfway between 26 and another number. What is the other number?

choices.misconception: I gave the gap from 20 to 26 instead of a number on the line.
I counted back 6 numbers from 20 but said 20 as the first one.
I found the number halfway between 20 and 26 instead.
I added 20 and 26 together instead of using the gap.

hints: How far is 26 from 20?
Halfway means the same distance on both sides. Find how far 26 is from 20, then go the same distance from 20 the other way.
26 is 6 more than 20, so the other number is 6 less than 20.

solutions.reliable: 26 is 6 steps above 20. The middle number must be the same distance from both ends, so the other number is 6 steps below 20: 20 - 6 = 14. Check: halfway between 14 and 26 is 20. The idea to keep: the middle of two numbers is equally far from each, so a known end and the middle tell you the other end.
solutions.elegant: Draw 20 in the middle with a jump of 6 to the right to reach 26. Copy the same jump to the left and you land on 14.

problems.whyOnTest: Working from the middle out to an end checks that you understand halfway as equal distances, not as a sum to halve.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nina shares 18 crayons equally between herself and her 2 friends. How many crayons does each of them get?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of children sharing instead of the crayons each one gets.
I shared the crayons between the 2 friends and forgot that Nina gets some too.
I took away 3 crayons, one for each child, instead of sharing them out.
I took away 2 crayons for the 2 friends instead of sharing.

hints: How many children are sharing?
Nina keeps a share too, so count her. Sharing equally means every child gets the same number, so think of 18 split into that many equal groups.
3 children share 18 crayons. How many 3s make 18?

solutions.reliable: Nina and her 2 friends make 3 children. 18 crayons shared into 3 equal groups is 6 in each group, because 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Each child gets a third of the crayons. The idea to keep: before sharing, count everyone who gets a share, including the person doing the sharing.
solutions.elegant: Deal the crayons out in rounds of one each: every round uses 3 crayons, and 6 rounds use all 18.

problems.whyOnTest: Equal sharing is the first meaning of a fraction, and forgetting to count the sharer is the classic trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The picture shows steps 1, 2 and 3 of a pattern of block staircases. How many blocks are in step 5?

figure.alt: Three staircases made of equal square blocks, labelled step 1, step 2 and step 3. Step 1 is a single block. Step 2 has columns of 1 and 2 blocks, 3 blocks in all. Step 3 has columns of 1, 2 and 3 blocks, 6 blocks in all.

choices.misconception: I found the blocks in step 4 and stopped one step too early.
I saw that step 3 added 3 blocks and kept adding 3 each time.
I went one step too far and found the blocks in step 6.
I thought step 5 would be a full square of 5 rows of 5 blocks.

hints: Count the blocks in each step. What is added each time?
Each new step puts a new column on the right that is one block taller than the column before. Keep adding columns until you reach step 5.
Steps 1, 2 and 3 have 1, 3 and 6 blocks. Step 4 adds a column of 4 blocks.

solutions.reliable: Step 1 has 1 block, step 2 has 1 + 2 = 3 and step 3 has 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Each step adds a column one taller than the last, so step 4 has 6 + 4 = 10 and step 5 has 10 + 5 = 15. The idea to keep: look at what each step adds, because the amount added can grow too.
solutions.elegant: Step 5 is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. Pair the ends: 1 + 4 = 5 and 2 + 3 = 5, plus the 5 itself, which makes 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

problems.whyOnTest: Growing patterns check whether you see what each step adds, and here the amount added grows by one every time.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Tom gives away half of his marbles. Now he has 6 marbles left. How many marbles did he give away?

choices.misconception: I took half of the 6 marbles he has left.
I added half of 6 to the 6 he has left.
I found how many marbles he had at the start, not how many he gave away.
I added the 6 he has left to the 12 he started with.

hints: If he gave away half, what is the other half?
Halving makes two equal parts: the part he gave away and the part he kept. Think about how big those two parts are compared with each other.
The 6 marbles he kept are one half. The marbles he gave away are the other half.

solutions.reliable: Half means two equal parts. The marbles he kept and the marbles he gave away are the two halves, so they are the same size. He kept 6, so he gave away 6. Check: he started with 6 + 6 = 12, and half of 12 is 6. The idea to keep: the two halves of something are always equal, so knowing one half tells you the other.

problems.whyOnTest: This checks that you understand halves as two equal parts, and the starting amount is the tempting wrong answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana, Ben and Cy sit in a row of 3 chairs. Ana does not want to sit next to Ben. In how many different orders can they sit?

choices.misconception: I thought that with only 3 chairs, Ana and Ben always end up next to each other.
I counted Ana, Cy, Ben and Ben, Cy, Ana as the same order, but they are different.
I counted the orders where Ana and Ben do sit next to each other.
I counted every order of the three children and forgot about the rule.

hints: List the orders, or think about the middle chair.
Write all the orders of three children in a fixed way, then cross out every order where Ana and Ben are side by side. Or ask yourself who can sit in the middle chair.
If Ana or Ben sits in the middle, the two of them are next to each other. So Cy must sit in the middle.

solutions.reliable: All the orders are ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB and CBA. Ana and Ben are side by side in ABC, BAC, CAB and CBA. That leaves ACB and BCA, so there are 2 orders. The idea to keep: list every case in a fixed order, then cross out the ones a rule forbids.
solutions.elegant: The middle chair touches both ends, so whoever sits there is next to everyone. It must be Cy. Then Ana sits on the left or on the right, which gives 2 orders.

problems.whyOnTest: A rule that forbids some orders checks careful listing, and the middle seat is the idea that makes it quick.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which number is 10 more than 38?

choices.misconception: I counted 10 down instead of 10 up.
I added 1 to 38 instead of adding 10.
I added 1 to both digits of 38.
I thought 10 more means writing a 0 on the end of the number.

hints: Which digit changes when you add 10?
Adding 10 adds one more ten. Only the tens digit goes up, and the ones digit stays the same.
38 has 3 tens and 8 ones. One more ten makes 4 tens and still 8 ones.

solutions.reliable: 38 is 3 tens and 8 ones. Adding 10 gives 4 tens and 8 ones, which is 48. The idea to keep: adding 10 raises the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit alone.
solutions.elegant: On a hundred square, 10 more is the square straight below, and below 38 is 48.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding 10 tests place value directly, and changing the ones digit instead is the common mistake.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A butterfly picture looks exactly the same on both sides of its middle line. Its left wing has 3 big spots and 2 small spots. How many spots does the whole butterfly have?

choices.misconception: I counted the spots on the left wing only.
I doubled the big spots and forgot about the small spots.
I doubled the small spots but counted the big spots only once.
I doubled the big spots but counted the small spots only once.

hints: What does the right wing look like?
Looking the same on both sides of a line means the right wing is a mirror copy of the left wing, with the same spots. Count one wing, then add its copy.
The left wing has 3 + 2 = 5 spots, and the right wing has the same number.

solutions.reliable: The right wing is a mirror copy of the left, so it also has 3 big and 2 small spots. Each wing has 5 spots, so the butterfly has 5 + 5 = 10. The idea to keep: a shape with a line of symmetry has two matching halves, so count one half and double it.

problems.whyOnTest: Line symmetry means two matching halves, and doubling only part of one half is the slip this catches.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Max uses each of the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 exactly once to make two two-digit numbers. Then he adds the two numbers. What is the biggest total he can get?

choices.misconception: I added the four digits instead of making two-digit numbers.
I made the smallest total instead of the biggest.
I made the biggest number, 43, first and then had only 2 and 1 left, so I added 43 and 21.
I made 43 and 34, but that uses the 4 and the 3 twice and leaves out 1 and 2.

hints: Which digits matter most in a two-digit number?
A tens digit is worth ten times as much as a ones digit. Put the two biggest digits in the tens places and the two smallest digits in the ones places.
Use 4 and 3 as the tens digits, which gives 40 + 30 = 70. The 2 and the 1 go in the ones places.

solutions.reliable: The tens digits count ten times over, so they should be 4 and 3, giving 70. The ones digits are then 2 and 1, adding 3 more. For example 42 + 31 = 73, and 41 + 32 = 73 too. No choice of tens digits beats 4 and 3, so 73 is the biggest. The idea to keep: put the biggest digits in the places worth the most.
solutions.elegant: The total is the two tens digits counted as tens plus the two ones digits. Making the tens digits 4 and 3 gives 70 + 3 = 73, whichever way the ones digits are placed.

problems.whyOnTest: Making the biggest total checks that you know a tens digit is worth more, and grabbing the biggest single number first is the trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: 9 girls and 6 boys come to a dance class. The teacher makes as many pairs as she can, and any two children can be a pair. How many children are left without a partner?

choices.misconception: I thought 9 and 6 add up to an even number, so everyone would get a partner.
I paired each girl with a boy, but any two children can be a pair.
I found how many pairs there are instead of how many children are left over.
I added the girls and boys and stopped without making any pairs.

hints: How many children are there altogether?
Since any two children can make a pair, only the total matters. Make pairs from the whole class and see whether the total is odd or even.
There are 9 + 6 = 15 children. Count in twos up to 15.

solutions.reliable: There are 9 + 6 = 15 children. Pairs use children two at a time: 7 pairs use 14 children, and 1 child is left. The idea to keep: an odd number of things always leaves one over when you put them in pairs.
solutions.elegant: The 6 boys make 3 pairs. 8 of the girls make 4 pairs, and 1 girl is left. Either way exactly one child has no partner, because 15 is odd.

problems.whyOnTest: Odd and even is about pairing, and the girl-with-boy reading is the trap that careful reading avoids.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ann has 7 pairs of socks and 1 extra sock without a partner. How many socks does she have?

choices.misconception: I counted the pairs and forgot that each pair has 2 socks and that there is an extra sock.
I counted the 7 pairs and the extra sock, but that counts pairs, not socks.
I counted the socks in the pairs and forgot the extra sock.
I added another whole pair for the extra sock instead of just one sock.

hints: How many socks are in one pair?
A pair is 2 socks, so count the socks in all the pairs by counting in twos. Then add the one sock that has no partner.
7 pairs is 7 groups of 2, which is 14 socks.

solutions.reliable: 7 pairs of 2 socks is 14 socks. The extra sock makes 14 + 1 = 15. The total is odd because one sock has no partner. The idea to keep: things in pairs always make an even number, and one left over makes it odd.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting in pairs and spotting the odd one out is the start of odd and even, and counting pairs instead of socks is the slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ella rolls a red die and a blue die. Each die shows a number from 1 to 6. In how many different ways can the two numbers add up to 9?

choices.misconception: I counted 3 and 6 and then 4 and 5, and forgot that the red and blue dice can swap their numbers.
I thought every number on the red die has a partner on the blue die, so I counted 6 ways.
I also counted 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 7 and 2, and 8 and 1, but a die only goes up to 6.
I thought there must be 9 ways because the total is 9.

hints: Start with the red die showing 1. Can the blue die show what you need?
Go through the red die’s numbers in order and find what the blue die must show each time. Cross out any case needing more than 6. Red 3 with blue 6 differs from red 6 with blue 3.
Red 1 needs blue 8 and red 2 needs blue 7, which a die cannot show. Red 3 needs blue 6, which works. Keep going up to red 6.

solutions.reliable: Red 1 would need blue 8 and red 2 would need blue 7, but a die only goes up to 6, so those do not work. Red 3 and blue 6, red 4 and blue 5, red 5 and blue 4, red 6 and blue 3 all work. That makes 4 ways. The idea to keep: fix one thing at a time and list in order, then check every case against the rules, here that a die shows only 1 to 6.
solutions.elegant: The biggest a die can show is 6, so each die must show at least 9 - 6 = 3. The red die can be 3, 4, 5 or 6, and each choice fixes the blue die, so there are 4 ways.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing ways to make a total checks systematic listing: go in order, treat the two dice as different, and drop the cases a die cannot show.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Sara reads 5 pages on Monday, 9 pages on Tuesday and 3 pages on Wednesday. How many more pages does she read on Tuesday than on Monday?

choices.misconception: I added the pages for all three days.
I added Monday and Tuesday instead of finding how many more.
I compared Tuesday with Wednesday instead of with Monday.
I gave the number of pages she read on Tuesday.

hints: Which two days does the question ask about?
Read the last sentence carefully. One of the days in the story is not needed. 'How many more' means you compare two amounts, so find the gap between them.
Compare Tuesday's 9 pages with Monday's 5 pages. Count on from 5 to 9.

solutions.reliable: The question compares Tuesday with Monday, so Wednesday is not needed. Tuesday has 9 pages and Monday has 5, and counting on from 5 to 9 takes 4 steps, so she reads 4 more pages on Tuesday. Check: 5 + 4 = 9. The idea to keep: read the question to the end before using numbers, because a story can include facts you do not need, and 'how many more' asks for a difference, not a total.
solutions.elegant: Line up 9 dots for Tuesday under 5 dots for Monday. Tuesday has 4 dots with no partner, so it is 4 more.

problems.whyOnTest: Contest stories often include a fact you do not need, and finding what is actually being asked keeps you from adding every number in sight.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana has 10 cards and Ben has 4 cards. How many cards must Ana give to Ben so that they both have the same number of cards?

choices.misconception: I had Ana give away half of her cards.
I found the difference, but giving 6 cards would leave Ana with fewer than Ben.
I found how many cards each of them ends up with, not how many Ana gives.
I gave the total number of cards they have together.

hints: When Ana gives a card, what happens to both of them?
Draw a bar for each child. Each card Ana gives makes her bar one shorter and Ben's bar one longer. Find the number they will both end up with first.
Together they have 14 cards, so each should end with 7. Ana has 10 now.

solutions.reliable: Together they have 10 + 4 = 14 cards, so to be equal each must have 7. Ana goes from 10 to 7, so she gives 3. Check: Ben goes from 4 to 7. The idea to keep: moving one thing from one side to the other changes both sides, so the gap closes by 2 for each card.
solutions.elegant: The gap is 10 - 4 = 6. Each card that moves closes the gap by 2, so 3 cards close a gap of 6.

problems.whyOnTest: Making two amounts equal checks the bar model idea that giving changes both amounts at once, so the difference is not the answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a club, 4 children play chess. That is a quarter of all the children in the club. How many children are in the club?

choices.misconception: I shared the 4 children into 4 equal parts.
I gave the number of children who play chess, not the whole club.
I doubled 4, as if a quarter were a half.
I counted only the children who do not play chess.

hints: A quarter is one of how many equal parts?
A quarter means the whole club is split into 4 equal groups, and the chess players fill one of them. Build the whole club from 4 groups that size.
One quarter is 4 children, so each of the 4 equal groups has 4 children.

solutions.reliable: A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. One part is 4 children, so the whole club is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 children. Check: a quarter of 16 is 4. The idea to keep: if you know one equal part, build the whole by putting all the parts back together.
solutions.elegant: Half the club is twice a quarter, 8 children, and the whole club is twice that, 16.

problems.whyOnTest: Going from a part back to the whole checks real understanding of a quarter, not just dividing by 4.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Four square tiles, each with sides of 1 cm, are put together edge to edge to make one shape. What is the smallest possible distance all the way round the shape?

choices.misconception: I counted the tiles instead of the edges around the outside.
I put the tiles in a row, but that is not the shape with the shortest way round.
I made a big square and took away each shared side once, but a shared side hides two edges.
I added up all the sides of all four tiles, including the sides that touch.

hints: Try a few shapes and count the outside edges of each.
Every time two tiles share a side, two edges are hidden from the outside. The shortest way round comes from the shape where the most sides are shared.
A row of four tiles shares 3 sides. A 2 by 2 square shares 4 sides.

solutions.reliable: The four tiles have 16 edges in all. Each shared side hides 2 edges. A row shares 3 sides, so it measures 16 - 6 = 10 cm round. A 2 by 2 square shares 4 sides, so it measures 16 - 8 = 8 cm round, and no shape of four tiles shares more than 4 sides. The smallest is 8 cm. The idea to keep: the more the tiles touch, the shorter the way round, so a square shape is best.
solutions.elegant: Draw the 2 by 2 square: each side is 2 cm, so the way round is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 cm. Every other shape of four tiles, like a row or an L, measures 10 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Same tiles, different shapes, different perimeters: this checks that you compare outside edges, not the number of tiles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ella folds a paper square in half and cuts 3 small shapes through both layers: 2 away from the fold, 1 right on the fold. How many holes are there when she opens it?

choices.misconception: I counted only the holes on one side of the fold and left out the hole on the fold.
I forgot that the scissors cut through both layers, so I counted one hole for each shape.
I counted two holes for each shape away from the fold and forgot the shape on the fold.
I thought every shape makes two holes, even the one cut right on the fold.

hints: What happens to a shape cut right on the fold?
The scissors go through both layers, so a shape away from the fold makes a hole on each half. A shape cut on the fold opens out into one hole across the fold. Count each kind.
The 2 shapes away from the fold make 2 holes each, which is 4 holes. The shape on the fold opens into just one hole.

solutions.reliable: Each shape away from the fold is cut through both layers, so it makes one hole on each half of the opened square: 2 shapes make 4 holes. The shape on the fold opens out into a single hole that crosses the fold, so it adds just 1. That makes 4 + 1 = 5 holes. The idea to keep: the fold works like a mirror, and a shape sitting on the mirror line is its own match.

problems.whyOnTest: Folding and cutting shows a line of symmetry at work: every hole has a partner across the fold, except one sitting on the fold.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Owen has an orange, a blue and a purple T-shirt, and black, white and grey shorts. He never wears orange with black. How many outfits of one T-shirt and shorts can he make?

choices.misconception: I took the orange T-shirt and the black shorts away completely, leaving 2 T-shirts and 2 shorts.
I added the 3 T-shirts and the 3 shorts instead of making pairs.
I took away the orange-with-black outfit twice, once for the T-shirt and once for the shorts.
I counted every outfit and forgot about the rule.

hints: Draw a tree: one branch for each T-shirt.
From each T-shirt, draw a branch for each pair of shorts. Count all the ends, then cross out any outfit the rule does not allow.
Each T-shirt goes with 3 shorts, so there are 3 x 3 outfits before the rule. The rule removes just one of them.

solutions.reliable: Each of the 3 T-shirts can go with each of the 3 shorts, which gives 9 outfits. The rule removes only orange with black, which is one outfit. That leaves 9 - 1 = 8. The idea to keep: count all the pairs first with a tree, then take away exactly the ones the rule forbids.
solutions.elegant: Count by T-shirt: orange goes with 2 shorts, blue with 3 and purple with 3, so 2 + 3 + 3 = 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Tree diagrams make every pair visible, and a rule that removes one pair checks you do not remove too much.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Zoe has three cards: 1, 2 and 4. She picks one, two or all three cards and adds the numbers. How many different totals can she get?

choices.misconception: I only counted the totals from picking two cards.
I forgot that she can pick just one card, so I counted only two cards and all three.
I forgot that she can pick all three cards together.
I also counted picking no cards, with a total of 0, but she must pick at least one.

hints: Sort your list by how many cards she picks.
List the totals for one card, then for two cards, then for all three. Then check whether any total appears twice, because the question asks for different totals.
One card gives 1, 2 and 4. Two cards give 3, 5 and 6. Now add all three.

solutions.reliable: One card: 1, 2, 4. Two cards: 1 + 2 = 3, 1 + 4 = 5, 2 + 4 = 6. Three cards: 7. The totals 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are all different, so there are 7. The idea to keep: list cases by size, one group at a time, and then check for repeats.
solutions.elegant: With the cards 1, 2 and 4 you can make every total from 1 up to 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, and each total only once, so there are 7.

problems.whyOnTest: Systematic listing by cases checks that no group of picks is forgotten, which is what each wrong total does.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lily and Max take turns writing 1, 2, 3 and so on, in order. Lily writes 1, Max writes 2, Lily writes 3, and they stop after 15. How many numbers does Max write?

choices.misconception: I took 14 - 2 = 12 and halved it, but that counts the gaps between Max's numbers, not the numbers.
I counted the numbers Lily writes instead of Max.
I gave the last number Max writes instead of how many numbers he writes.
I counted all the numbers they write together.

hints: Does Max write the odd numbers or the even numbers?
Lily writes every odd number and Max writes every even number. List Max's numbers up to 15 and count them, or put the numbers into pairs.
Max writes 2, 4, 6 and so on. The last even number before 15 is 14.

solutions.reliable: Max writes the even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14. That is 7 numbers. The idea to keep: taking turns splits the numbers into odd and even, and an odd stopping number means the first player writes one more.
solutions.elegant: Pair the numbers: (1, 2), (3, 4) and so on up to (13, 14). Each pair gives Max one number, and there are 7 pairs. The 15 is left over for Lily.

problems.whyOnTest: Taking turns is a hidden odd and even question, and counting gaps instead of numbers is the off-by-one trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A square table seats one person on each side. Three of these tables are pushed together in a row to make one long table. How many people can sit at it?

choices.misconception: I counted only the people along the two long sides and forgot the two ends.
I took away one seat for each table instead of two seats for each place the tables touch.
I took away only one seat where two tables touch, but two seats are lost there.
I gave each table 4 seats and forgot that seats are lost where tables touch.

hints: Draw the three tables in a row.
Draw the long table and put a dot for each seat. Where two tables touch, the sides pressed together have no room for anyone, so those seats disappear.
Along each long side there is one seat per table, so 3 on each side. Then look at the two ends.

solutions.reliable: Drawing it, each long side has 3 seats, one for each table, which makes 6, and each end has 1 seat, which makes 2 more. That is 8 people. The idea to keep: draw the picture, because joining things together hides some edges and the drawing shows exactly which.
solutions.elegant: Three tables have 12 sides. They touch in 2 places, and each place hides 2 sides, so 12 - 4 = 8 seats are left.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing a quick diagram turns a trap into a count, and the joined sides are what make 12 wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: There are 7 frogs on lily pads and 5 frogs in the water. Then 4 frogs jump from the water onto the lily pads. How many frogs are on the lily pads now?

choices.misconception: I found how many frogs are still in the water.
I took the 4 frogs away from the lily pads instead of adding them.
I counted all the frogs in the pond.
I added all the numbers, so I counted the 4 jumping frogs twice.

hints: Which group gets bigger, and which gets smaller?
The frogs that jump leave the water and join the frogs on the lily pads. The question only asks about the lily pads.
7 frogs were already on the lily pads, and 4 more arrive.

solutions.reliable: The lily pads start with 7 frogs and 4 more jump on, so there are 7 + 4 = 11. Check: the water now has 5 - 4 = 1 frog, and 11 + 1 = 12 frogs in all, the same as before. The idea to keep: when things move from one group to another, one part grows, the other shrinks, and the whole stays the same.

problems.whyOnTest: Moving things between two parts checks that you track which part the question is about while the total stays fixed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: On a number line, Lia stands exactly 4 steps away from 9. Which of these numbers could she be standing on?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of steps instead of a number on the line.
I counted back 4 numbers from 9 but said 9 as the first one: 9, 8, 7, 6.
I counted on 4 numbers from 9 but said 9 as the first one: 9, 10, 11, 12.
I multiplied 4 by 9 instead of taking steps on the line.

hints: Could Lia be on the left of 9 as well as on the right?
Draw a number line and mark 9. Take 4 steps one way and see where you land, then take 4 steps the other way. Do not count 9 itself as a step.
4 steps to the right of 9 is 13, which is not a choice. Now try 4 steps to the left.

solutions.reliable: 4 steps to the right of 9 is 9 + 4 = 13, and 4 steps to the left of 9 is 9 - 4 = 5. Lia could be on 13 or on 5. Only 5 is in the list, so the answer is 5. The idea to keep: a distance on a number line can go either way, so check both sides of the starting number.
solutions.elegant: Jump back 4 from 9: 8, 7, 6, 5. Each number you say is one step, and the fourth one is 5.

problems.whyOnTest: Distance on a number line can go in both directions, and checking only one side, or counting the starting number as a step, are the slips this catches.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many different two-digit numbers can be written using only the digits 5 and 7? A digit may be used twice, as in 55.

choices.misconception: I only made 57, writing the digits in the order they were given.
I used each digit only once, so I found only 57 and 75.
I counted 57 and 75 as the same number, but they are different.
I also counted the one-digit numbers 5 and 7.

hints: Choose the tens digit first.
List the numbers in order: pick the tens digit, then the ones digit. Each place can be 5 or 7, and the same digit can be used in both places.
With 5 in the tens place you get 55 and 57. Now put 7 in the tens place.

solutions.reliable: With 5 in the tens place: 55 and 57. With 7 in the tens place: 75 and 77. That makes 4 numbers. The idea to keep: fill one place at a time and list every choice for it, so nothing is missed.
solutions.elegant: There are 2 choices for the tens digit and 2 for the ones digit, so 2 x 2 = 4 numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Listing numbers from given digits checks a system for counting, and forgetting repeated digits is the common miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 7 to the power 100 is divided by 5?

choices.misconception: I reduced 7 to 2 correctly but then used a remainder of 1 when dividing 100 by 4.
I read the cycle backwards and landed on the entry before the right one.
I used 100 divided by 4 giving 25 and read off the 25th entry as if the cycle had length 25.
I assumed a power that large must be divisible by 5.

hints: Replace 7 by its remainder on division by 5 before doing anything else.
7 leaves 2, so 7^100 leaves the same remainder as 2^100. Now find the cycle of 2 modulo 5.
2, 4, 3, 1 repeats with length 4, and 100 is a multiple of 4, so the remainder is the last entry: 1.

solutions.reliable: First reduce the base: 7 leaves remainder 2 on division by 5, so 7^100 and 2^100 leave the same remainder. Now find the cycle of powers of 2 modulo 5: 2, 4, 8 -> 3, 16 -> 1, and then it repeats. The cycle is 2, 4, 3, 1 with length 4. Since 100 = 4 x 25 is an exact multiple of 4, the exponent lands on the LAST entry of the cycle, giving remainder 1. The transferable idea: reduce the base first, then find the cycle length, then locate the exponent within it.

problems.whyOnTest: Reducing the base before finding the cycle is what keeps these arithmetic-free, and an exact multiple landing on the last entry is the usual off-by-one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the size of one interior angle of a regular twelve-sided polygon?

choices.misconception: I found the exterior angle and answered with that instead of the interior one.
I used 360 divided by 12 subtracted from 195, or otherwise slipped a step in the arithmetic.
I gave the total of all twelve interior angles rather than one of them.
I used a ten-sided polygon by mistake.

hints: The exterior angles of any polygon always add to 360 degrees.
Each exterior angle of a regular 12-gon is 360 / 12 = 30 degrees.
Interior and exterior angles sit on a straight line, so the interior angle is 180 - 30 = 150 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360 degrees, so in a regular twelve-sided figure each exterior angle is 360 / 12 = 30 degrees. An interior angle and its exterior angle lie on a straight line, so the interior angle is 180 - 30 = 150 degrees. Cross-check with the other formula: the interior angles total (12 - 2) x 180 = 1800 degrees, and 1800 / 12 = 150. The transferable idea: the exterior route is shorter and almost always safer.
solutions.elegant: Exterior angles share 360 degrees twelve ways, giving 30 each, so the interior angle is 150.

problems.whyOnTest: Answering with the exterior angle, or with the total rather than one angle, are the two errors this question is built to catch.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence is defined by a(1) = 2 and a(n+1) = 2 a(n) - 1 for every n. What is a(6)?

choices.misconception: I used the rule 2a(n) - 1 but started the sequence at 1 instead of 2.
I doubled six times and ignored the minus one entirely.
I stopped at a(5), one term early.
I computed 2^6 - 1, applying the minus one only once at the very end.

hints: Just generate the terms one at a time; six is not many.

solutions.reliable: Generate the terms directly: a1 = 2; a2 = 2 x 2 - 1 = 3; a3 = 2 x 3 - 1 = 5; a4 = 2 x 5 - 1 = 9; a5 = 2 x 9 - 1 = 17; a6 = 2 x 17 - 1 = 33. With only six terms wanted there is no reason to look for a closed form, and doing so is where mistakes creep in. If you do want one, notice each term is one more than a power of two: a(n) = 2^(n-1) + 1, and 2^5 + 1 = 33. The transferable idea: when only a few terms are wanted, generating them beats deriving a formula.
solutions.elegant: Each term is one more than a power of 2, so a(6) = 2^5 + 1 = 33.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules reward just computing, and the marks are lost by reaching for a formula or stopping one term short.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A committee of 4 must be formed from 5 boys and 4 girls, and it must contain exactly 2 boys and 2 girls. How many different committees are possible?

choices.misconception: I chose any 4 from all 9 people and ignored the two-and-two requirement.
I added the two counts instead of multiplying them.
I treated the choices as ordered, counting the same committee several times.
I used 5 x 4 x 2 or a similar shortcut rather than counting each selection properly.

hints: Choose the boys and the girls as two separate jobs.
The number of ways to pick 2 boys from 5 is 5 choose 2, and 2 girls from 4 is 4 choose 2.
5 choose 2 = 10 and 4 choose 2 = 6, and the two choices are independent, so 10 x 6 = 60.

solutions.reliable: Split the task into two independent choices. Picking 2 boys from 5 can be done in C(5,2) = (5 x 4)/2 = 10 ways. Picking 2 girls from 4 can be done in C(4,2) = (4 x 3)/2 = 6 ways. Every choice of boys can pair with every choice of girls, so the multiplication principle gives 10 x 6 = 60 committees. The transferable idea: independent choices multiply, and only mutually exclusive cases add.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding when you should multiply, and ignoring a composition constraint, are the two errors that account for most lost marks here.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each of the four edges of a square is painted either black or white. Two paintings count as the same if one can be rotated onto the other. How many genuinely different paintings are there?

choices.misconception: I counted every colouring of the four edges and forgot that rotations make some of them identical.
I divided 16 by 4, but that only works when no painting is left unchanged by a rotation, and some are.
I halved 16, treating only the 180 degree turn as a symmetry.
I listed by how many edges are black but forgot that two black edges can be adjacent or opposite.

hints: Some paintings survive a turn unchanged.
Group the paintings by how many edges are black: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4.
Zero black: 1 way. One black: 1. Two black: 2 (adjacent or opposite). Three black: 1. Four black: 1. Total 1+1+2+1+1 = 6.

solutions.reliable: Divide-by-four fails here, because some paintings are unchanged by a rotation, so classify by hand instead. Group by the number of black edges. All white: 1 painting. Exactly one black edge: any single edge can be rotated to any other, so 1. Exactly two black: the two black edges are either adjacent or opposite, and rotation cannot turn one into the other, so 2. Exactly three black: 1, by the same argument as one. All black: 1. The total is 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6. The transferable idea: when symmetry is involved, case-splitting on an invariant feature - here the number of black edges - is safer than dividing.
solutions.elegant: The count of black edges survives any rotation, so classify by it and only the two-black case splits, into adjacent and opposite.

problems.whyOnTest: Dividing by the number of symmetries is the standard trap, and it is wrong exactly when some object is fixed by a symmetry.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A driver travels from one town to another at an average of 60 km/h and returns along the same road at an average of 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two speeds, which would only be right if equal TIME were spent at each, not equal distance.
I weighted the two speeds by their own values instead of by the time each leg took.
I halved the correct answer, dividing by the total distance twice.
I added the two speeds together, which gives a number faster than either leg and so cannot be an average of them.

hints: Average speed is never the average of two speeds.
Pick a convenient distance, say 120 km each way, and work out the two times.
120/60 = 2 hours out and 120/40 = 3 hours back, so 240 km in 5 hours, which is 48 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Average speed means total distance divided by total time, and here the two legs take different times, so the two speeds cannot simply be averaged. Choose a convenient one-way distance - 120 km works because both speeds divide it - giving 120/60 = 2 hours out and 120/40 = 3 hours back. That is 240 km in 5 hours, so the average is 240/5 = 48 km/h. Notice it is below the midpoint of 50, because more of the journey's TIME is spent at the slower speed. Any distance gives the same answer. The transferable idea: average speed is total distance over total time, and equal distances weight the slower leg more heavily.
solutions.elegant: Equal distances at two speeds give their harmonic mean: 2 x 60 x 40 / (60 + 40) = 4800/100 = 48.

problems.whyOnTest: The plain average is the trap, and knowing the answer must fall below it eliminates two choices instantly.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the smallest number n such that ANY collection of n whole numbers must contain two of them whose difference is divisible by 7?

choices.misconception: I used the number of possible remainders without adding one for the pair that must collide.
I doubled 7, thinking I needed two full sets of remainders.
I doubled 7 and added one, applying the pigeonhole idea to the wrong number of boxes.
I guessed from small cases without identifying what the boxes actually are.

hints: Two numbers differ by a multiple of 7 when their remainders agree.
There are only 7 possible remainders: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Those are the pigeonholes.
Seven numbers could have all seven different remainders, so seven is not enough. Eight numbers must repeat a remainder, so n = 8.

solutions.reliable: The difference of two numbers is divisible by 7 precisely when the two leave the same remainder on division by 7. There are exactly 7 possible remainders, so treat those as boxes. With 7 numbers you could get one in each box - for example 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, no two of which differ by a multiple of 7 - so 7 is not enough. With 8 numbers there are more numbers than boxes, so some box holds two, and those two differ by a multiple of 7. The answer is 8. The transferable idea: identify the boxes precisely, then the answer is boxes plus one.
solutions.elegant: Seven remainders are seven pigeonholes, so the eighth number forces a repeat.

problems.whyOnTest: Naming the pigeonholes correctly is the whole problem; once they are remainders modulo 7 the answer is immediate.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: An 8 by 8 chessboard has two opposite corner squares removed, leaving 62 squares. Each domino covers exactly two squares that share an edge. Can the 62 squares be covered exactly by 31 dominoes?

choices.text: No, because the two removed corners share a colour, so 32 squares of one colour remain and only 30 of the other
Yes, because 62 is even and 31 dominoes cover exactly 62 squares
choices.misconception: I checked that the counts match but a matching count does not make a covering possible.

choices.text: No, because 62 is not divisible by 4
choices.misconception: I invented a divisibility condition; dominoes cover two squares, so only divisibility by 2 could matter.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the dominoes may be placed diagonally
choices.misconception: I changed the rules rather than testing them; the question says dominoes cover squares sharing an edge.

choices.text: No, because the board is no longer rectangular
choices.misconception: I appealed to the shape, but plenty of non-rectangular regions can be tiled by dominoes.

hints: Colour the board like a real chessboard and look at what each domino must cover.
Every domino covers exactly one black and one white square, whatever its position or orientation.
Opposite corners of a chessboard share a colour, so removing them leaves 32 of one colour and 30 of the other - and 31 dominoes would need 31 of each.

solutions.reliable: Colour the board in the usual alternating pattern. Because neighbouring squares always differ in colour, every domino - however placed - covers exactly one square of each colour. So 31 dominoes must cover 31 black and 31 white squares. Now, the two opposite corners of a chessboard are always the SAME colour. Removing them leaves 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other, which no set of 31 dominoes can match. The covering is therefore impossible. The transferable idea: a colouring turns an impossible search over arrangements into a single counting statement.
solutions.elegant: Every domino takes one square of each colour, and the mutilated board has 32 of one and 30 of the other.

problems.whyOnTest: This is the cleanest example of a colouring argument, where proving impossibility is easier than any amount of searching.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many diagonals does a convex polygon with 12 sides have? A diagonal joins two vertices that are not already joined by a side.

choices.misconception: I counted every line joining two vertices and forgot to remove the 12 sides.
I counted each diagonal from both of its endpoints and forgot to halve.
I used 12 x 10 without halving, double counting every diagonal.
I subtracted 24 rather than 12, removing each side twice.

hints: Count from each vertex, then think about how many times each diagonal got counted.
From any one of the 12 vertices you can draw a diagonal to 9 others: not to itself, and not to its two neighbours.
That gives 12 x 9 = 108 endpoint-counts, but each diagonal has two endpoints, so divide by 2 to get 54.

solutions.reliable: From a single vertex, you can reach 11 other vertices, but two of them are its neighbours and those lines are sides, not diagonals. So each vertex is the endpoint of 12 - 3 = 9 diagonals. Multiplying gives 12 x 9 = 108, but this counts every diagonal twice, once from each end, so the true number is 108 / 2 = 54. Equivalently: all C(12,2) = 66 vertex pairs, minus the 12 that are sides, gives 66 - 12 = 54. The transferable idea: whenever you count from each object, ask how many times the thing you want has been counted.
solutions.elegant: All 66 vertex pairs minus the 12 that are sides leaves 54 diagonals.

problems.whyOnTest: Forgetting to halve is the standard error, and having a second method that agrees is the fastest way to catch it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the remainder when 3 to the power 2024 is divided by 13?

choices.misconception: I treated 2024 as a multiple of the cycle length 3 and read off the end of the cycle.
I gave the remainder of 2024 divided by the cycle length 3, instead of 3 squared.
I used a remainder of 1 where dividing 2024 by 3 actually leaves 2.
I divided 2024 by 12 using Fermat's little theorem and gave the remainder 8 instead of 3 to the power 8.

hints: Find the smallest power of 3 that leaves remainder 1.
Compute powers of 3 modulo 13 until the remainder returns to 1. That gives the cycle length, and the exponent's remainder on division by it picks the answer.
3 cubed is 27, which leaves remainder 1, so the cycle has length 3, and 2024 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3.

solutions.reliable: Since 3 cubed is 27 and 27 leaves remainder 1 on division by 13, the powers of 3 repeat with period 3. As 2024 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3, the answer matches 3 squared, which is 9. The transferable idea: find the first exponent returning to remainder 1, because that period controls every larger exponent.
solutions.elegant: 2024 = 3 x 674 + 2, so 3 to the 2024 behaves exactly like 3 squared.

problems.whyOnTest: Modular cycles are the only route to exponents this size, and the cycle length has to be discovered rather than assumed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many four-member teams can be chosen from ten people?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the ten people by the four places, which counts neither orderings nor selections.
I divided the 5040 ordered picks by 4 instead of by 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24.
I counted the ordered selections and never divided out the orderings within a team.
I allowed each of the four places to be filled by any of the ten, repeating people.

hints: A team has no internal order.
Count the ordered picks first, then divide by the number of ways the chosen four could be arranged, since each team was counted once for every arrangement.
10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040 ordered picks, and each team of four appears 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 times.

solutions.reliable: Ordered picks give 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040, and each team appears in all 24 of its orderings, so the count is 5040 / 24 = 210. The transferable idea: overcount in a way you can measure exactly, then divide by that measured overcount.
solutions.elegant: Choosing four to include is the same as choosing six to leave out, so the two calculations must agree.

problems.whyOnTest: Selections are arrangements divided by the internal orderings, and the undivided count is the distractor that catches a rushed answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a regular pentagon, two diagonals are drawn from the same vertex. What is the angle between them?

choices.misconception: I took the interior angle as 360 / 5 = 72 and split that into three.
I assumed the interior angle was 90 degrees and divided it into three.
I divided the interior angle by two rather than into the three equal parts the diagonals create.
I used the exterior angle of the pentagon rather than the angle between the diagonals.

hints: The two diagonals cut the interior angle into equal parts.
Find the pentagon's interior angle, then notice that the two diagonals from one vertex divide it into three equal angles because the triangles they create are congruent.
The interior angle of a regular pentagon is 108 degrees, and it is split into three equal pieces.

solutions.reliable: A regular pentagon's interior angle is 108 degrees, and the two diagonals from a vertex split it into three equal angles by symmetry, each 36 degrees. The transferable idea: in a regular polygon, use symmetry to divide a known angle rather than computing each piece from scratch.
solutions.elegant: 36 is a fifth of 180, which is why the regular pentagon is full of 36 and 72 degree angles.

problems.whyOnTest: Pentagon angle chases are standard in the 4-point block, and halving the interior angle instead of thirding it is the usual slip.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten different positive integers add to 100. What is the largest the smallest of them can be?

choices.misconception: I stopped one step early after finding that a smallest value of 4 was achievable.
I ignored that ten different integers starting at 6 already exceed 100.
I divided 100 by 10 and stepped down one to leave room for the numbers to differ, without checking the total.
I divided 100 by 10 and used that, forgetting the numbers have to differ from each other.

hints: Push the smallest up and see what the others are forced to be.
If the smallest is s, the ten different integers are at least s, s + 1, up to s + 9, so their total is at least ten times s plus forty-five. Compare that bound with 100.
Ten times s plus 45 must not exceed 100, which forces s to be at most five and a half.

solutions.reliable: If the smallest is s, the ten distinct values total at least 10s + 45. Requiring 10s + 45 to be at most 100 gives s at most 5, and 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 19 shows 5 is reached. The transferable idea: bound the quantity first, then construct one example meeting the bound, because an extremal answer needs both halves.
solutions.elegant: The tightest ten distinct integers from s are forced, so the bound is a single inequality.

problems.whyOnTest: Extremal questions need a bound and a construction, and every distractor here comes from supplying only one of the two.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One pipe fills a tank in 4 hours and another in 6 hours. An open drain empties it in 12 hours. With all three open, how long does filling take?

choices.misconception: I added the drain's rate instead of subtracting it, so all three pipes seemed to fill the tank.
I added the two filling rates and ignored the drain completely.
I averaged the two filling times, 4 and 6, and ignored the drain.
I added the two filling times, 4 + 6, and ignored the drain.

hints: Turn every pipe into a fraction of the tank per hour.
Write each pipe's contribution as tank per hour, make the drain negative, add all three, then take the reciprocal of the total to get the time.
One quarter plus one sixth minus one twelfth of the tank fills each hour.

solutions.reliable: Per hour the pipes add 1/4 and 1/6 and the drain removes 1/12, so the net rate is 3/12 + 2/12 - 1/12 = 1/3 of the tank per hour, and filling takes 3 hours. The transferable idea: rates add with signs while times do not, so a drain is simply a negative rate.
solutions.elegant: Working in twelfths of a tank makes the three numbers 3, 2 and minus 1, which total 4 twelfths.

problems.whyOnTest: A drain in the problem makes signed rates essential, and ignoring it or subtracting times gives two of the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence begins 1, 1 and each later term is the sum of the two before it. How many of the first twenty terms are divisible by 3?

choices.misconception: I checked only the small terms, where multiples of 3 are still rare.
I found the pattern but counted one occurrence short across twenty positions.
I assumed every third term was divisible by 3, matching the divisor to the spacing.
I assumed half the terms would be divisible, with no pattern behind the guess.

hints: Replace each term by its remainder on division by three.
Work the recursion entirely in remainders modulo 3. The remainders repeat in a short block, and counting the zeros in that block across twenty positions gives the answer.
The remainders run 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0 and then repeat every eight terms.

solutions.reliable: Taking the recursion modulo 3 gives remainders 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, repeating with period 8, so a zero appears at every fourth position. Among the first twenty terms the fourth, eighth, twelfth, sixteenth and twentieth are divisible by 3, which is five. The transferable idea: run a recursion in remainders and the terms become a short cycle.
solutions.elegant: Zeros sit at every fourth position, so twenty terms hold twenty divided by four of them.

problems.whyOnTest: Fibonacci-style terms outgrow any calculator quickly, and working modulo the divisor is the only finishable route.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Different numbers are chosen from 1 to 10. How many must be chosen to be certain that two of them add to 11?

choices.misconception: I assumed the first two chosen would pair up, which is possible but not certain.
I counted the pairs that add to 11 and gave that count rather than one more.
I assumed every number had to be chosen before a pair was guaranteed.
I added one to the ten numbers rather than to the five pairs.

hints: Group the numbers into the pairs that add to eleven.
The ten numbers split into pairs summing to 11. Choosing at most one from each pair avoids a match, so the answer is one more than the number of pairs.
The pairs are 1 with 10, 2 with 9, 3 with 8, 4 with 7 and 5 with 6.

solutions.reliable: The numbers fall into the five pairs 1 and 10, 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6. Five numbers can avoid a pair by taking one from each, but a sixth must complete one, so six is needed. The transferable idea: build the pigeonholes out of the forbidden condition itself, then take one more than the number of holes.
solutions.elegant: Five holes and six items settles it with no case checking at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Pigeonhole arguments in the 5-point block turn on finding the right pigeonholes, and the count of holes is always offered instead of the answer.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The midpoints of a triangle's three sides are joined to make a smaller triangle. What fraction of the original area does it cover?

choices.misconception: I cubed the length ratio, which would be right for volumes rather than areas.
I assumed the original split into three equal pieces rather than four.
I used the length ratio directly instead of squaring it.
I gave the area of the three corner triangles rather than the middle one.

hints: Compare one side of each triangle.
Each side of the inner triangle is half the side it is parallel to, so the triangles are similar with length ratio one half. Areas scale by the square of that ratio.
Lengths halve, so areas are multiplied by one half squared.

solutions.reliable: The midpoint triangle is similar to the original with every side halved, so its area is one half squared, a quarter. The three corner triangles make up the other three quarters, each also a quarter. The transferable idea: similar figures scale area by the square of the length ratio, which is why halving the sides quarters the area.
solutions.elegant: The four pieces are all congruent, so each is a quarter without any ratio being squared.
