problems.statement: A 5 by 5 grid holds 25 lamps, all switched off. A move flips every lamp in one whole row, or every lamp in one whole column: lamps that were on go off and lamps that were off come on. Which of these could be the number of lamps that are on after some moves?

choices.misconception: I flipped one row and one column and counted 5 + 5 - 1 = 9, forgetting that the lamp where they cross is flipped twice and goes back off.
I thought the 16 lamps around the border could be lit, without checking that no set of row and column moves gives that pattern.
I flipped four rows for 20 lamps, then a column, and thought the column only lit the one lamp in the fifth row, forgetting it also turns four lamps off.
I thought every lamp except one corner could be lit, but every 2 by 2 block always has an even number of lamps on, and the corner block would have 3.

hints: Does the order of the moves matter? What does flipping the same row twice do?
A lamp's final state depends only on whether its row and its column were each flipped an odd number of times. Say r rows and c columns are flipped once; count lit lamps using r and c.
A lamp is on exactly when one of its row and its column is flipped but not both, so the number on is r(5 - c) + c(5 - r). Try the values of r and c from 0 to 5.

solutions.reliable: Flipping a row twice undoes it, and the order of the moves does not matter, so the result depends only on which r rows and which c columns are flipped an odd number of times. A lamp is on exactly when its row or its column is flipped, but not both, which gives r(5 - c) + c(5 - r) lamps on. Running through r and c from 0 to 5 gives only 0, 5, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 20 and 25. Of the choices only 14 appears, from r = 3 and c = 1: 3 x 4 + 1 x 2 = 14. The transferable idea: when moves can be done in any order and cancel in pairs, describe every reachable state by which moves were used an odd number of times.
solutions.elegant: Any 2 by 2 block of lamps, taken from two rows and two columns, always has an even number on, because every move flips 0 or 2 of its lamps. That rules out 24 at once, and the formula r(5 - c) + c(5 - r) settles the rest.

problems.whyOnTest: Seeing that the moves commute and cancel in pairs turns a huge search into one formula, and the 2 by 2 parity invariant rules out almost-full patterns.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 24 are written on a board. A move erases two of the numbers, a and b, and writes the single number √(a^2 + b^2) in their place. After 23 moves only one number is left. What is it?

choices.misconception: I treated √(a^2 + b^2) as if it were just the larger of a and b, so I expected the largest number, 24, to survive.
I assumed the sum of the numbers stays the same, so I added up the numbers 1 to 24 and got 300.
I found the quantity that stays fixed, the sum of the squares, but forgot to take its square root at the end.

choices.text: It depends on the order of the moves
choices.misconception: I tried two different orders on a few numbers, got messy square roots, and decided the result must change with the order.

hints: Look for something that a move does not change.
A move replaces a and b by a number whose square is a^2 + b^2. Compare the sum of the squares of all the numbers on the board before and after a move.
The sum of the squares never changes, so the last number squared equals 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 24^2 = 24 x 25 x 49 / 6.

solutions.reliable: Before a move the two numbers contribute a^2 + b^2 to the sum of the squares of all the numbers on the board, and afterwards the new number contributes (√(a^2 + b^2))^2 = a^2 + b^2. So the sum of the squares never changes. At the start it is 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 24^2 = 24 x 25 x 49 / 6 = 4900. At the end the single number x satisfies x^2 = 4900, so x = 70. The transferable idea: when a move combines numbers, look for a quantity, often a sum of some function of the numbers, that the move leaves unchanged.
solutions.elegant: Try a small case: 3 and 4 become 5, and 9 + 16 = 25. That shows the sum of the squares is what survives, whatever the order, so only the starting sum of squares matters.

problems.whyOnTest: The invariant here is the sum of the squares, and the problem tests whether a solver looks for what stays fixed instead of simulating 23 moves.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A large cube is built from 27 small cubes, 3 along each edge. A worm eats every small cube exactly once, each time moving on to a small cube that shares a face with the one it has just eaten. How many of the 27 small cubes could be the first one it eats?

choices.misconception: I thought the worm must start at a corner, so I counted only the 8 corner cubes.
I coloured the cubes in two alternating colours and counted the colour with 13 cubes, not the colour with 14 that the path must start on.
I thought only the hidden centre cube was a bad place to start, and that every other cube would work.
I thought any cube could be the start, since the worm can turn in any direction it likes.

hints: Colour the small cubes in two colours, like a three-dimensional chessboard.
Cubes sharing a face always get different colours, so the worm's route alternates colours. Count each colour, and ask which colour a route through all 27 cubes must begin on.

The colour of the corners has 14 cubes, the 8 corners and the 6 face centres, and the other colour has 13. A route of 27 cubes alternating colours uses 14 of one and 13 of the other, starting and ending on the colour with 14.

solutions.reliable: Colour each small cube black or white so that cubes sharing a face have different colours, with the corners black. The black cubes are the 8 corners and the 6 face centres, 14 in all; the white cubes are the 12 edge middles and the centre, 13 in all. The worm's 27 cubes alternate in colour, so the 1st, 3rd, ..., 27th cubes share one colour (14 cubes) and the other 13 cubes have the other colour. So the first cube must be black. Every black cube does work. From a corner, snake through the bottom 3 by 3 layer, step up, snake through the middle layer, step up and snake through the top layer. From a face centre, spiral out from the centre of that face's layer to a corner, then step up and snake through the other two layers in the same way. So the answer is 14. The transferable idea: in a route that alternates two colours through an odd number of cells, the start and the end must be on the colour that has one more cell.

problems.whyOnTest: A two-colouring shows a route through an odd number of cells must start on the majority colour, and the distractors count the wrong colour or skip the colouring.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A board has 4 rows and 7 columns of squares. One square is removed, and the remaining 27 squares are to be covered exactly by nine 1 by 3 tiles, each lying along a row or down a column. How many of the 28 squares could be the removed one?

choices.misconception: I checked that removing a corner works and assumed that only the four corners could be removed.
I used one diagonal colouring with three colours and counted the 10 squares of the colour that appears most, without also using the colouring along the other diagonals.
I used a chessboard colouring and thought the removed square must be black, but a 1 by 3 tile does not cover one square of each of two colours.
I only checked that 27 is a multiple of 3, so I thought any square could be removed.

hints: Colour along diagonals with three colours, so every tile covers each colour once.
Give the square in row r, column c the colour (r + c) mod 3. Each tile covers every colour once, so the removed square has the colour with one extra square. Repeat with (r - c) mod 3.
Numbering rows 1 to 4 and columns 1 to 7, both colourings single out the squares in rows 1 and 4 and columns 1, 4 and 7. Check that each of these really works.

solutions.reliable: Colour the square in row r and column c with colour (r + c) mod 3. A 1 by 3 tile, across or down, always covers one square of each colour. The board has 10 squares of one colour (the colour of the top-left corner) and 9 of each of the others, so for the 27 remaining squares to split 9, 9, 9 the removed square must have that colour. The same argument with colour (r - c) mod 3 gives a second condition. With rows numbered 1 to 4 and columns 1 to 7, the squares passing both tests are those in rows 1 and 4 and columns 1, 4 and 7: six squares. Each of them works: if the removed square is in the top row, the rest of that row splits into pieces of length 3, and the 3 by 7 block below is filled by seven upright tiles; the bottom row is the same upside down. So the answer is 6. The transferable idea: colour so that every tile covers each colour equally; the missing square must then come from the colour in surplus, and two different colourings can be combined.

problems.whyOnTest: Tiling questions with 1 by 3 tiles are settled by a three-colouring along diagonals, and using both diagonal directions is what cuts 10 candidates down to 6.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Each equation below has exactly one real solution x. For how many of the five equations is that solution a fraction p/q, where p and q are whole numbers? 4^x = 8, 8^x = 4, 2^x = 3, 9^x = 27, 6^x = 24.

choices.misconception: I looked only for whole-number solutions, and none of the five equations has one, so I counted none.
I solved 4^x = 8 and 8^x = 4 by writing everything as powers of 2, but did not notice that 9 and 27 are both powers of 3.
I saw that 6^x = 24 needs x a little less than 2 and guessed x = 7/4 without checking, but 6^(7/4) is only about 23, not 24.
I thought every equation like these must have a fraction as its solution, because any real number can be written as one.

hints: Write both sides of each equation as powers of the same prime where you can.
4^x = 8 becomes 2^(2x) = 2^3, and 9^x = 27 works the same way with 3. For 2^x = 3, suppose x = p/q and raise both sides to the power q. What goes wrong?
If 2^(p/q) = 3 then 2^p = 3^q, but the left side is even and the right side is odd. For 6^x = 24, x = p/q gives 2^p x 3^p = 2^(3q) x 3^q, so p = 3q and p = q at once.

solutions.reliable: Three equations can be solved directly. 4^x = 8 is 2^(2x) = 2^3, so x = 3/2. 8^x = 4 is 2^(3x) = 2^2, so x = 2/3. 9^x = 27 is 3^(2x) = 3^3, so x = 3/2. For 2^x = 3, the solution is between 1 and 2, so it is positive. Suppose it were a fraction p/q with p and q positive whole numbers. Raising 2^(p/q) = 3 to the power q gives 2^p = 3^q, but 2^p is even and 3^q is odd, a contradiction. For 6^x = 24, the solution is again positive, and x = p/q would give 6^p = 24^q, that is 2^p x 3^p = 2^(3q) x 3^q. Each prime must appear to the same power on both sides, so p = 3q and p = q, which forces q = 0, another contradiction. So exactly 3 of the solutions are fractions. The transferable idea: to show a number is not a fraction, assume it is p/q, clear the fraction, and find a clash such as even equals odd.
solutions.elegant: An equation a^x = b with whole numbers a and b has a fraction solution exactly when a and b are powers of one common number, because a^p = b^q forces the same primes, in the same proportions, on both sides. 4 and 8, 8 and 4, 9 and 27 pass this test, while 2 and 3, and 6 and 24, fail it: 3 answers.

problems.whyOnTest: Proving that a number is not a fraction is the classic proof by contradiction: assume x = p/q, clear the denominator and reach a clash, here even against odd or two different powers of the same prime.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers cannot be written as x^2 - y^2, where x and y are positive integers?

choices.misconception: I only tried 2024 = 1 x 2024 as (x - y)(x + y), saw that the two factors had different parities, and gave up instead of trying 2 x 1012.
I thought a perfect square can only be written with y = 0, which is not allowed, and missed 1013^2 - 1012^2.
I thought a prime cannot be split as (x - y)(x + y), forgetting the factor pair 1 x 2027.
I stretched the rule too far and thought numbers that are 4 times an odd number fail, just like numbers that are 2 times an odd number.

hints: Factor x^2 - y^2 and think about the parities of the two factors.
x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y), and x - y and x + y always have the same parity. So the number must be a product of two odd numbers or of two even numbers.
Two odd factors give an odd product; two even factors give a multiple of 4. A number that is even but not a multiple of 4 can be neither.

solutions.reliable: x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y), and the two factors differ by 2y, which is even, so they have the same parity. If both are odd the product is odd; if both are even it is a multiple of 4. So a number that is 2 more than a multiple of 4 is impossible, and 2022 = 4 x 505 + 2 is such a number. The others all work: 2024 = 507^2 - 505^2, 2025 = 1013^2 - 1012^2, 2027 = 1014^2 - 1013^2 and 2028 = 508^2 - 506^2. The transferable idea: assuming a representation exists and reaching a parity clash is a proof by contradiction that it does not.
solutions.elegant: Squares leave remainder 0 or 1 on division by 4, so a difference of two squares leaves remainder 0, 1 or 3, never 2. Only 2022 leaves remainder 2.

problems.whyOnTest: Showing a number is not a difference of squares uses factor parity or squares mod 4, and every distractor is a number that someone wrongly rules out.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A train 160 m long travels at 72 km/h and crosses a bridge 440 m long. How many seconds pass from the moment the front of the train reaches the bridge until the back of the train leaves it?

choices.misconception: I only used the length of the train, 160 m, as the distance travelled.
I subtracted the train's length from the bridge, 440 - 160 = 280 m, as if the train only had to be wholly on the bridge.
I used only the bridge's 440 m and forgot that the train must also travel its own length to clear it.
I changed 72 km/h into metres per second by dividing by 60 only, getting 1.2 m/s instead of 20 m/s.

hints: Follow the back of the train: how far does it travel?
Put the speed into metres per second first. The front must cross the whole bridge, and then the rest of the train must follow it off.
72 km/h is 72 000 m in 3600 s, which is 20 m/s, and the distance is 160 + 440 = 600 m.

solutions.reliable: 72 km/h = 72 000 m / 3600 s = 20 m/s. From the front reaching the bridge to the back leaving it, the back of the train travels the length of the bridge plus the length of the train, 440 + 160 = 600 m. The time is 600 / 20 = 30 seconds. The transferable idea: convert to matching units before dividing, and track one fixed point on a moving object to see the real distance.

problems.whyOnTest: Unit conversion and reading exactly which moment ends the crossing decide this, and each distractor is a slip in one of the two.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A regular tetrahedron ABCD has every edge 6 cm long. M is the midpoint of edge AB and N is the midpoint of the opposite edge CD. An ant walks on the surface of the tetrahedron from M to N. What is the length of the shortest possible walk?

choices.misconception: I measured the straight line from M to N through the inside of the tetrahedron, which the ant cannot use.
I measured from M across face ABC to the corner C, and forgot that the ant still has to go along CD to reach N.
I walked from M across face ABC to the corner C and then along edge CD to N, which bends at C instead of going straight.
I kept the ant on the edges, going from M to A, then along AD to D and then along DC to N, which is 3 + 6 + 3.

hints: M and N lie on different pairs of faces, so the ant crosses an edge.

Choose two faces that share an edge, for example ABC and ACD, which share AC. Unfold them flat: they form a rhombus made of two equilateral triangles, and the shortest walk is a straight segment in it.
In the rhombus, M and N are the midpoints of two opposite sides, AB and CD. Put A at (0, 0) and C at (6, 0): then M = (1.5, -1.5√3) and N = (4.5, 1.5√3).

solutions.reliable: M is on faces ABC and ABD, and N is on faces ACD and BCD, so the walk must cross one of the edges AC, AD, BC or BD. By symmetry all four choices give the same length, so take the walk across AC. Unfold faces ABC and ACD into the plane along AC: they form a rhombus of two equilateral triangles with side 6. Put A = (0, 0) and C = (6, 0); then B = (3, -3√3) and D = (3, 3√3), so M = (1.5, -1.5√3) and N = (4.5, 1.5√3). The straight segment MN crosses AC at its midpoint (3, 0), so it stays inside the two faces, and its length is √(3^2 + (3√3)^2) = √(9 + 27) = 6 cm. This beats the routes through a corner, such as 3√3 + 3, about 8.2 cm. The transferable idea: for a shortest walk on a solid, unfold the faces the walk passes through into one flat piece and join the two points with a straight line.
solutions.elegant: In the unfolded rhombus ABCD, MN joins the midpoints of the opposite sides AB and CD, so it is parallel to the other two sides and as long as them: 6 cm.

problems.whyOnTest: Shortest walks on the surface of a solid become straight lines once the right faces are unfolded into a flat net, and each distractor either leaves the surface or bends at a corner.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are placed in a 3 by 3 grid, one in each square. A number is called a peak if it is larger than every number in a square sharing an edge with it. What is the smallest possible number of peaks?

choices.misconception: I thought a clever arrangement could have no peak at all, forgetting that 9 is larger than everything next to it.
I thought 9 and 8 are always both peaks, but 8 is not a peak when it sits next to 9.
I thought the three largest numbers, 9, 8 and 7, are always peaks because only each other can beat them.
I found the largest possible number of peaks, with big numbers in the corners and the centre, instead of the smallest.

hints: Which number is certain to be a peak, wherever it goes?
Think about the largest number in the grid: nothing beside it can beat it. Then try to arrange the others so that each of them has a bigger neighbour.
9 is always a peak, so the answer is at least 1. Try a snake: 1, 2, 3 along the top row, 6, 5, 4 in the middle row, 7, 8, 9 along the bottom row.

solutions.reliable: The number 9 is larger than all its neighbours wherever it is placed, so there is always at least one peak. One peak is possible: put 1, 2, 3 in the top row, 6, 5, 4 in the middle row and 7, 8, 9 in the bottom row. Each number from 1 to 8 then shares an edge with the number one larger than it, so none of them is a peak, and only 9 is. The smallest possible number of peaks is 1. The transferable idea: the largest element of a finite set always has an extreme property, which gives a lower bound for free.

problems.whyOnTest: The largest number must be a peak, which is the extremal principle, and a snake arrangement shows that one peak is enough.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers is the largest?

choices.misconception: I picked the number with the largest exponent, without allowing for its small base.
I saw that 2^600 = (2√2)^400 is smaller than 3^400, then assumed 5^300 and 11^200 must be smaller still because their exponents are smaller.
I picked the number with the largest base, without allowing for its smaller exponent.
I noticed that 2^600 = 4^300 = 8^200 and assumed every choice was the same number written in a different way.

hints: Write every number as something to the power 100.
2^600 = (2^6)^100, and the others can be rewritten in the same way. Once the exponents match, only the bases need comparing.
The four numbers are 64^100, 81^100, 125^100 and 121^100.

solutions.reliable: Rewrite each number with exponent 100: 2^600 = (2^6)^100 = 64^100, 3^400 = (3^4)^100 = 81^100, 5^300 = (5^3)^100 = 125^100 and 11^200 = (11^2)^100 = 121^100. With equal exponents the largest base wins, so 5^300 is the largest, just ahead of 11^200, and the numbers are clearly not all equal. The transferable idea: to compare powers, rewrite them with a common exponent or a common base instead of trying to estimate their size.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparing huge powers is instant after spotting a common exponent and hopeless by grinding, and the near tie between 125 and 121 punishes guessing.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A frog climbs a staircase of 10 steps. Each jump takes it up either 1 step or 2 steps, and it never makes two 2-step jumps one straight after the other. In how many different ways can it get from the bottom to the top step?

choices.misconception: I worked out 1, 2, 3 and 4 ways for staircases of 1, 2, 3 and 4 steps and assumed the pattern goes on as n ways for n steps.
I found the right rule and built the list 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 28, but stopped after nine terms, which is the count for 9 steps.
I sorted the routes by the number of 2-step jumps and counted 1 + 9 + 21 for none, one and two of them, but forgot that three 2-step jumps can also be kept apart.
I ignored the rule about two 2-step jumps in a row and counted every route made of 1-step and 2-step jumps.

hints: Count the ways for 1 to 6 steps first. The early pattern does not last.
Look at the last jump. If it is a 1-step jump, what is left is any good route up n - 1 steps. If it is a 2-step jump, the jump before must be a 1-step jump, or none.
So the number of ways w(n) satisfies w(n) = w(n - 1) + w(n - 3), with w(1) = 1, w(2) = 2 and w(3) = 3.

solutions.reliable: Let w(n) be the number of good routes up n steps. Small cases give w(1) = 1, w(2) = 2 (1+1 and 2) and w(3) = 3 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1). For n of at least 4, split by the last jump. If it is a 1-step jump, the rest is any good route up n - 1 steps: w(n - 1) ways. If it is a 2-step jump, the jump before it is a 1-step jump, so the route ends with 1 then 2, and what comes before is any good route up n - 3 steps: w(n - 3) ways. So w(n) = w(n - 1) + w(n - 3), which gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 28, 41. The answer is 41. Notice that the first four terms, 1, 2, 3, 4, look like the counting numbers, but the fifth is 6, not 5. The transferable idea: small cases suggest a pattern, but only the structure behind them, here a rule for the last jump, tells you how it continues.
solutions.elegant: Count by the number k of 2-step jumps. Then there are 10 - 2k one-step jumps, and the 2-step jumps must go into different gaps among them, of which there are 11 - 2k. That gives 1 + 9 + 21 + 10 = 41 for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, since C(9, 1) = 9, C(7, 2) = 21 and C(5, 3) = 10, while k = 4 or 5 is impossible.

problems.whyOnTest: Small cases are the way in, but 1, 2, 3, 4 suggests a false pattern, so the test is finding the rule behind the cases and checking it with a second count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Given that 2^10 = 1024, how many digits does the number 2^100 have?

choices.misconception: I used 2^10 as about 10^3 to get 2^100 as about 10^30, and thought 10^30 has 30 digits, but it has 31.
I used the rougher estimate 2^3 as about 10, which makes 2^100 about 10^33.3 and suggests 34 digits, but 2^3 is only 8.
I thought each doubling adds half a digit, so 100 doublings make 50 digits.
I thought each doubling adds one digit, so 100 doublings make 100 digits.

hints: Write 2^100 as a power of 1024.
2^100 = 1024^10 = 1.024^10 x 10^30. Decide roughly how big 1.024^10 is, and remember how many digits a power of 10 has.
1.024^10 is about 1.27: more than 1 and far less than 10. So 2^100 is between 10^30 and 10^31.

solutions.reliable: 2^100 = (2^10)^10 = 1024^10 = 1.024^10 x 10^30. The factor 1.024^10 is about 1.27, roughly 1 + 10 x 0.024 plus a little, so it is more than 1 and certainly less than 10. Hence 2^100 lies between 10^30 and 10^31. Every number from 10^30 up to just below 10^31 has 31 digits, so 2^100 has 31 digits. The transferable idea: estimate a huge power as a power of ten times a factor you can bound, and remember that 10^k has k + 1 digits.
solutions.elegant: Since log 2 is about 0.301, 2^100 is about 10^30.1, and the number of digits is the whole-number part of 30.1 plus one: 31.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting the digits of a huge power is an estimation task, and the classic slips are the off-by-one in the digits of 10^k and an estimate that is too rough.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the three numbers rolled is a multiple of 4?

choices.misconception: I worked out the probability that the product is not a multiple of 4, and gave that instead.
I thought the product is a multiple of 4 only when at least one die shows a 4, so I worked out 1 - (5/6)^3.
I counted the cases with at least two even dice, but forgot that a single 4 with two odd dice also works.
I only made sure the product is even, which needs just one even die, giving 1 - 1/8.

hints: Count the cases where the product fails to be a multiple of 4.
The product fails when all three dice are odd, or when exactly one die is even and that die shows 2 or 6. Find both probabilities, subtract from 1, then check by counting the successes directly.
All odd: 1/8. Exactly one die even and it shows 2 or 6: 3 x (1/3) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. So the product fails with probability 3/8.

solutions.reliable: Work with the complement. The product is not a multiple of 4 when it has at most one factor of 2. That happens if all three dice are odd, with probability (1/2)^3 = 1/8, or if exactly one die shows 2 or 6 and the other two are odd, with probability 3 x (2/6) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. So the product fails with probability 1/8 + 1/4 = 3/8, and the answer is 1 - 3/8 = 5/8. Check directly: at least two even dice has probability 1/2, and exactly one even die that shows 4 has probability 3 x (1/6) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/8, giving 1/2 + 1/8 = 5/8 again. The transferable idea: when two methods agree you can trust the answer, and when they disagree the difference shows which case was missed.

problems.whyOnTest: Probability with divisibility needs careful cases, and a second method by complement catches the single-4 case that a direct count tends to miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the last digit of 2^1 + 2^2 + 2^3 + ... + 2^2026?

choices.misconception: I noticed that each block of four powers ends in 2 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 20, so I assumed the whole sum ends in 0 and ignored the leftover terms.
I split the sum into blocks of four but counted only one leftover term, 2^2025, which ends in 2.
I counted three leftover terms after the blocks of four and added 2 + 4 + 8 = 14.
I used the formula 2^2027 - 2 but forgot to subtract the 2, so I gave the last digit of 2^2027.

hints: The last digits of the powers of 2 repeat in a short cycle.
The last digits go 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, 8, 6, ... Group the terms in blocks of four and see what is left over after the last full block.
Each block of four adds a last digit of 0. Since 2026 = 4 x 506 + 2, two terms are left over, ending in 2 and 4.

solutions.reliable: The last digits of 2^1, 2^2, 2^3 and 2^4 are 2, 4, 8 and 6, and the cycle repeats every four powers. Each full block contributes 2 + 4 + 8 + 6 = 20, which ends in 0. Since 2026 = 4 x 506 + 2, there are 506 full blocks and two leftover terms, 2^2025 and 2^2026, ending in 2 and 4. So the sum ends in 0 + 2 + 4 = 6. The transferable idea: for the last digit of a long sum, group the terms by the cycle and handle the leftover terms carefully.
solutions.elegant: The sum equals 2^2027 - 2. Since 2027 = 4 x 506 + 3, the number 2^2027 ends in 8, so the sum ends in 8 - 2 = 6.

problems.whyOnTest: Last-digit cycles make a 2026-term sum quick, and the distractors are the classic slips with the leftover terms.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the sum AB + BC + CA = ABC, each letter stands for a digit. AB, BC and CA are two-digit numbers, so AB has tens digit A and units digit B, and ABC is a three-digit number. What is the number ABC?

choices.misconception: I found that the digit sum A + B + C is 18 and gave that instead of the number ABC.
I reached B + 10C = 89 but then read it as B = 8 and C = 9, the digits of 89 in order.
I found the digits 1, 9 and 8 correctly but wrote them down in the reverse order.
I tried A = 2 and A = 3, found that B + 10C would have to be over 100, and stopped without trying A = 1.

hints: Write each two-digit number in terms of its digits.
Expand both sides: the left side is 11 times A + B + C. Collect the terms into one equation linking A, B and C, then use the fact that B and C are single digits.
11A + 11B + 11C = 100A + 10B + C simplifies to B + 10C = 89A, and the left side is at most 99.

solutions.reliable: AB + BC + CA = (10A + B) + (10B + C) + (10C + A) = 11(A + B + C), and ABC = 100A + 10B + C. Setting them equal gives B + 10C = 89A. The left side is at most 9 + 90 = 99, so A = 1 and B + 10C = 89, which forces C = 8 and B = 9. Check: 19 + 98 + 81 = 198. So ABC = 198. The transferable idea: in a letter sum, expand by place value, simplify, and then use the fact that digits lie between 0 and 9 to pin them down.
solutions.elegant: The left side is 11 times the digit sum, so ABC must be a multiple of 11 that equals 11 times its own digit sum. 198 = 11 x 18 with 1 + 9 + 8 = 18 fits at once, and the equation B + 10C = 89A shows it is the only one.

problems.whyOnTest: Place-value expansion turns a letter puzzle into one equation and digit bounds finish it; the distractors come from misreading digits or stopping early.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts with a(1) = 1 and a(2) = 2. After that, each term is found from the two before it by the rule a(n + 2) = (a(n + 1) + 1) / a(n). So a(3) = (2 + 1) / 1 = 3. What is the sum of the first 2026 terms?

choices.misconception: I found that the sequence repeats and worked out the 2026th term, 1, instead of the sum of the first 2026 terms.
I found that every five terms add up to 9 and that 2026 = 5 x 405 + 1, but I forgot the one leftover term.
I divided 2026 by 5 and rounded up to 406 full cycles, so 406 x 9 counted four terms that are not in the sum.
I noticed the terms 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 are centred on 2 and took the average term to be 2, but the average of one cycle is 9/5.

hints: Work out the next few terms carefully. They stay whole numbers.
The terms go 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1, 2, ... Each term depends only on the two before it, so the sequence repeats once two consecutive terms repeat. Find the cycle length and the sum of one cycle.
The cycle is 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, of length 5 and sum 9. Since 2026 = 5 x 405 + 1, there is one term left over after the full cycles.

solutions.reliable: Compute: a(3) = (2 + 1)/1 = 3, a(4) = (3 + 1)/2 = 2, a(5) = (2 + 1)/3 = 1, a(6) = (1 + 1)/2 = 1 and a(7) = (1 + 1)/1 = 2. So a(6) and a(7) equal a(1) and a(2), and since each term depends only on the two before it, the sequence repeats with period 5: 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, ... One cycle sums to 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9. As 2026 = 5 x 405 + 1, the first 2026 terms are 405 full cycles plus one more term, a(2026) = a(1) = 1. The sum is 405 x 9 + 1 = 3646. The transferable idea: a rule that uses only the last two terms starts repeating as soon as a pair of consecutive terms comes back, so find the period and handle the remainder.

problems.whyOnTest: A two-term rule that repeats is a recursive-pattern question in disguise: find the period, then handle the terms left over after the full cycles, which is where every distractor slips.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A jug holds 10 litres of a drink that is 50% juice. Some of the drink is poured out and replaced by the same amount of water. Then the same amount is poured out again and again replaced by water. The drink is now 32% juice. How many litres were poured out each time?

choices.misconception: I treated the two pourings as one, so I solved 1 - x/10 = 0.64.
I set the fraction poured out equal to 32/50 = 0.64, so I poured out 6.4 litres.
I halved the fraction kept, 0.64, because there were two pourings, so I solved 1 - x/10 = 0.32.
I found that each pouring keeps 0.8 of the juice and gave 0.8 x 10 = 8 litres, which is the amount kept, not the amount poured out.

hints: What fraction of the juice survives one pouring?
If x litres are poured out, the fraction of the juice that stays is 1 - x/10, and the same fraction stays the second time. So the juice percentage is multiplied by the same factor twice.

solutions.reliable: Pouring out x litres of the well-mixed drink removes the fraction x/10 of the juice and leaves the fraction 1 - x/10; adding water does not change the amount of juice. After two rounds the juice is 5 x (1 - x/10)^2 litres in 10 litres, so 50% x (1 - x/10)^2 = 32%. Then (1 - x/10)^2 = 0.64, so 1 - x/10 = 0.8 and x = 2. Check: after the first round 4 litres of juice remain, which is 40%; after the second, 3.2 litres remain, which is 32%. The transferable idea: repeated replacement multiplies the concentration by the same factor each time, so the factor appears squared.

problems.whyOnTest: Repeated dilution is multiplicative, so the key step is a square root; the distractors treat the process as a single step or misread what was asked.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In trapezium ABCD, side AB is parallel to side CD, AB = 4 cm and CD = 12 cm. The diagonals AC and BD meet at P. Triangle ABP has area 3 cm^2. What is the area of the trapezium, in cm^2?

choices.misconception: I scaled areas by the side ratio 3 instead of its square, making triangle CDP 9, and with side triangles of 9 each got 3 + 9 + 9 + 9.
I thought the two side triangles have the same area as the small triangle ABP, giving 3 + 27 + 3 + 3.
I found triangles ABP, CDP and BCP but forgot the fourth triangle, DAP, giving 3 + 27 + 9.
I took each side triangle to be the average of 3 and 27, which is 15, giving 3 + 27 + 15 + 15.

hints: Triangles ABP and CDP are similar. What is the scale factor?
The scale factor is 3, so P divides each diagonal in the ratio 1 : 3. Use this for the area of CDP, and also for the triangles BCP and DAP, which share a height with ABP.
Triangle CDP has area 9 x 3 = 27. Triangle BCP has base PC, three times PA, and the same apex B as triangle ABP, so its area is 9; so is the area of DAP.

solutions.reliable: Since AB is parallel to CD, triangles ABP and CDP are similar with ratio AB : CD = 1 : 3. So CDP has area 3^2 x 3 = 27 cm^2, and PC = 3 x PA. Triangles ABP and CBP have bases PA and PC on the same line AC and the same apex B, so CBP has 3 times the area of ABP, which is 9 cm^2. In the same way DAP has area 9 cm^2. The total is 3 + 27 + 9 + 9 = 48 cm^2. Check: the height of ABP from P to AB is h with (1/2) x 4 x h = 3, so h = 1.5; the trapezium's height is 4h = 6, and its area is (4 + 12)/2 x 6 = 48. The transferable idea: lengths scale by k and areas by k^2, and triangles with the same apex have areas in the ratio of their bases.
solutions.elegant: The two side triangles always have equal areas, and each is the geometric mean of the other two: √(3 x 27) = 9. So the total is 3 + 27 + 9 + 9 = 48.

problems.whyOnTest: Similar triangles in a trapezium test both the k^2 rule for areas and the shared-height rule, and each distractor breaks one of them.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A machine turns 6 into 12, 7 into 8, 8 into 15, 9 into 13 and 10 into 18. Following the same rule, what does it turn 12 into?

choices.misconception: I worked out that the machine is about divisors, but I counted the divisors of 12 instead of adding them.
I added the divisors of 12 but left out 12 itself, getting 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16.
I noticed that 8 goes to 15 and 10 goes to 18, and continued the even inputs by adding 3, so 12 goes to 21.
I saw that 6 goes to 12 and assumed the machine doubles, without checking the other examples.

hints: Look at 7 becoming 8. What could turn a prime into one more than itself?
Primes stand out: 7 becomes 7 + 1. Try listing the divisors of each input and doing something with them.
The machine adds up all the divisors of the input, including 1 and the number itself: 9 gives 1 + 3 + 9 = 13.

solutions.reliable: Test the idea suggested by 7 becoming 8, the sum of all divisors. For 6: 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 12. For 7: 1 + 7 = 8. For 8: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. For 9: 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. For 10: 1 + 2 + 5 + 10 = 18. All five fit. The divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, with sum 28. The transferable idea: when a rule must be inferred, start from the most unusual example, here a prime, and then check the guess against every example, not just one.

problems.whyOnTest: Inferring a rule means checking a guess against every example, and each distractor fits only one or two of the examples.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A drawer holds 10 red, 8 blue, 6 green and 4 black socks. In the dark, you take socks out one at a time. What is the smallest number you must take to be certain of having two pairs of different colours? A pair means two socks of the same colour.

choices.misconception: I found how many socks guarantee one pair, four colours plus one, and stopped there.
I took the five socks that guarantee one pair and added two more for the second pair.
I took all 10 red socks, then one more sock and then one more to finish, forgetting that the other colours could each give one sock without making a pair.
I found the worst case, 10 red socks and one of each other colour, and gave its size instead of adding one more sock.

hints: Imagine the most unlucky order of socks possible.
In the worst case you collect as many socks as possible while still having pairs in only one colour. Make that bad collection as large as you can, then add one.
The worst case is all 10 red socks plus one blue, one green and one black: 13 socks with pairs in only one colour.

solutions.reliable: To have pairs in at most one colour, you can hold any number of socks of one colour but at most one sock of each of the other three. The largest such collection uses the biggest colour: 10 red plus 1 blue, 1 green and 1 black, which is 13 socks. So 13 socks are not enough. With 14 socks it is impossible to have pairs in only one colour, since that allows at most 13 socks. The answer is 14. The transferable idea: for a guarantee, build the largest collection that still fails, then add one.

problems.whyOnTest: Worst-case counting needs the largest failing collection, and here that uses the biggest colour, which is the step most solvers miss.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a class of 30 students, 18 are in the chess club, 15 are in the choir and 4 are in neither. How many students are in exactly one of the two?

choices.misconception: I found the number of students in both, 7, and gave that instead of the number in exactly one.
I found the students in the chess club only, 18 - 7 = 11, and forgot those in the choir only.
I gave the number in at least one of the two, 30 - 4 = 26, which still includes the students in both.
I added 18 and 15 without noticing that some students were counted twice.

hints: First find how many students are in at least one of the two.
Students in at least one group: the total minus those in neither. Compare this with 18 + 15 to find how many were counted twice, which is the number in both.
26 students are in at least one group, and 18 + 15 = 33, so 7 are in both.

solutions.reliable: 30 - 4 = 26 students are in at least one group. Adding 18 + 15 = 33 counts the students in both groups twice, so 33 - 26 = 7 are in both. In exactly one group: 26 - 7 = 19. Check: chess only is 18 - 7 = 11 and choir only is 15 - 7 = 8, and 11 + 8 = 19. The transferable idea: inclusion-exclusion gives the overlap, and exactly one means at least one minus both.
solutions.elegant: Exactly one = (18 + 15) - 2 x 7 = 19, because the students in both groups appear twice in 33 and must be removed completely.

problems.whyOnTest: Two-set counting hinges on the overlap, and this question asks for exactly one, so every intermediate count appears among the choices.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm, and the length of each of its sides is a whole number of centimetres. How many different values can its area take?

choices.misconception: I also counted a 0 by 15 rectangle, with area 0, which is not a real rectangle.
I counted a 3 by 12 rectangle and a 12 by 3 rectangle separately, so I counted each area twice.
I counted every whole number from 1 to 15 as a possible side length.
I found the largest possible area, 7 x 8 = 56, instead of the number of different areas.

hints: What do the length and the width add up to?
Length plus width is 15. List the pairs of whole-number sides with the shorter side first, and check whether any two pairs give the same area.
The pairs are 1 and 14, 2 and 13, and so on up to 7 and 8, with areas 14, 26, 36, 44, 50, 54 and 56.

solutions.reliable: Half the perimeter is 15, so length + width = 15. With the shorter side first, the possibilities are 1 x 14, 2 x 13, 3 x 12, 4 x 11, 5 x 10, 6 x 9 and 7 x 8, with areas 14, 26, 36, 44, 50, 54 and 56. These are all different, so the area can take 7 different values. The transferable idea: read whether the question asks for a count of shapes, a count of values or a single value, and list without repeats.
solutions.elegant: The area a(15 - a) grows steadily as the shorter side a goes from 1 to 7, so the 7 choices of the shorter side give 7 different areas.

problems.whyOnTest: The question asks for a count of different areas, so solvers who count ordered pairs or report the biggest area answer a different question.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A machine turns 3 into 10, 5 into 26, 7 into 50 and 10 into 101. Using the same rule, which number does the machine turn into 82?

choices.misconception: I fitted the rule 'multiply by 3 and add 1' to the first example only, then undid it: (82 - 1) / 3.
I fitted the rule 'double and add 4' to the first example only, then undid it: (82 - 4) / 2.
I treated squaring as if it were doubling, so to work backwards I simply halved 82.
I undid the 'add 1' step but forgot to undo the squaring.

hints: Compare each output with the square of its input.
Find a rule that fits all four examples, not just the first one. Then run the machine backwards, undoing its steps in reverse order.
Each output is one more than the square of the input, for example 10 = 3 x 3 + 1.

solutions.reliable: Checking all four examples: 3 x 3 + 1 = 10, 5 x 5 + 1 = 26, 7 x 7 + 1 = 50 and 10 x 10 + 1 = 101, so the rule is 'square, then add 1'. For the output to be 82, the square must be 81, so the input is 9. The transferable idea: test a rule against every example, then reverse it by undoing the last step first.

problems.whyOnTest: Simple rules fit the first example alone, so the question checks that a rule fits every example and that you can run it backwards.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two snowploughs start at the same moment from opposite ends of a road and clear it towards each other, each at its own steady rate. They meet after 2 hours, and by then the first plough has cleared 3/5 of the road. How long would the second plough take to clear the whole road on its own?

choices.misconception: I multiplied 2 hours by 2/5 instead of dividing by it.
I took the 2/5 that the second plough cleared as its amount per hour, so I divided 1 by 2/5.
I worked out the time for the first plough alone, 2 hours divided by 3/5.
I thought that if two ploughs meet after 2 hours, each one alone would take twice as long.

hints: What fraction of the road did the second plough clear in those 2 hours?
Together the two ploughs cleared the whole road, so the second cleared the rest. At a steady rate, its fraction of the road and its time are in proportion, so scale up to the whole road.
The second plough cleared 2/5 of the road in 2 hours, which is 1/5 of the road per hour.

solutions.reliable: When they meet, the road is fully cleared, so the second plough cleared 1 - 3/5 = 2/5 of it in 2 hours. That is 1/5 of the road per hour, so the whole road would take 5 hours. The transferable idea: in a meeting problem the shares of the work add up to one whole, and each worker's share divided by the time gives its rate.
solutions.elegant: 2/5 of the road takes 2 hours, so each fifth takes 1 hour and all five fifths take 5 hours.

problems.whyOnTest: Rates appear as fractions of a job, and the distractors come from dividing the wrong way or answering for the wrong plough.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts with 1. Each later term is the previous term plus the sum of the digits of the previous term. So it begins 1, 2, 4, 8, ... What is the 10th term?

choices.misconception: I added only the last digit of each term instead of the sum of all its digits.
I lost count of the terms and gave the ninth term.
I treated 2 as the first term, so the term I called the 10th was really the 11th.
I assumed the doubling at the start carries on, giving 2 to the power 9.

hints: Write the terms out carefully, numbering them as you go.
A recursive rule like this has no shortcut, so the reliable method is to apply it one step at a time. The doubling at the start stops once the terms have two digits, so do not extend that pattern.
After 8 come 8 + 8 = 16, then 16 + 7 = 23, then 23 + 5 = 28.

solutions.reliable: Apply the rule: 1, 2, 4, 8, then 8 + 8 = 16, 16 + 7 = 23, 23 + 5 = 28, 28 + 10 = 38, 38 + 11 = 49 and 49 + 13 = 62. Counting, 62 is the 10th term. The transferable idea: early terms can suggest a false pattern, so with a recursive rule keep applying the rule itself and number the terms as you write them.

problems.whyOnTest: The opening 1, 2, 4, 8 invites a doubling guess, and the question checks whether you follow the rule rather than the first pattern you see.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A closed path is drawn along the lines of squared paper. It never crosses or touches itself, and it turns through a right angle at every corner. Which of these could be the number of corners of the path?

choices.misconception: I pictured a right-angled triangle, forgetting that its sloping side cannot run along the grid lines.
I imagined a rectangle with one corner cut away by a small step, and counted the step as only one extra corner.
I thought a plus-sign shape has 13 corners, counting its centre as well as the 12 real corners.
I thought any number of corners from 4 upwards could be made with enough zigzags.

hints: Look at the direction of each side as you go round.

At every right-angle turn the path switches between horizontal and vertical. Think about what that switching forces on the total number of sides, and so of corners, once the path returns to its start.
Going round, the sides run horizontal, vertical, horizontal, vertical, ... and the last side must join up with the first.

solutions.reliable: Every corner is a right-angle turn, so the sides alternate horizontal, vertical, horizontal, vertical. The path is closed, so its last side meets its first, and the sides pair up into horizontal-vertical pairs. So the number of sides is even, and the number of corners equals the number of sides. This rules out 3, 5, 13 and 15. Ten corners are possible: take a rectangle and cut a small square notch out of three of its corners, since each notch turns one corner into three. The transferable idea: when something alternates between two states and returns to where it began, the number of steps is even.

problems.whyOnTest: A parity argument settles it in one line, while trying to draw a shape for each option wastes time and invites miscounting.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Solve the equation x/(x - 2) = 2/(x - 2) + 3. Which of these is correct?

choices.misconception: I rearranged x = 3x - 4 as x - 3x = 4, a sign slip, and got x = -2.
I expanded 3(x - 2) as 3x - 2, which gave x = 3x and so x = 0.
I solved the equation after clearing the fractions and did not check that x = 2 makes both denominators zero.
I cancelled the (x - 2) from the two fractions, which left x = 2 + 3.

hints: Whatever you find, put it back into the original equation.
Multiplying both sides by x - 2 clears the fractions, but that step is only allowed when x - 2 is not zero. So any answer must be checked in the equation as it was first written.
Clearing the fractions gives x = 2 + 3(x - 2), so x = 3x - 4.

solutions.reliable: Multiply both sides by x - 2: x = 2 + 3(x - 2) = 3x - 4, so 2x = 4 and x = 2. But x = 2 makes both denominators zero, so it is not allowed, and the algebra gave no other candidate. The equation has no solution. The transferable idea: multiplying by an expression that can be zero may create a false solution, so always substitute back.
solutions.elegant: Move the fractions together: x/(x - 2) - 2/(x - 2) = (x - 2)/(x - 2), which equals 1 for every allowed x. Since 1 is never 3, there is no solution.

problems.whyOnTest: The algebra produces x = 2 smoothly, and only checking it against the original denominators shows it is not a real solution.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The mean score of a class on a test was 70. The five highest scorers had a mean of 90. The mean of the rest of the class was 66. How many students are in the class?

choices.misconception: I divided the 24-point gap between the top five and the rest by the 4-point gap between the rest and the class mean.
I took the 20-point gap between the top five's mean and the class mean as the number of students.
I found how many students were left after the top five were removed and gave that.
I reached 4n = 120 and forgot to divide by 4.

hints: Compare each group's mean with the class mean of 70.
A whole-class mean balances its parts: the total amount by which the top five sit above 70 must equal the total amount by which the others sit below 70.
The top five are each 20 above the mean, 100 in all. Each of the others is 4 below it.

solutions.reliable: Let n be the number of students. Writing the total score two ways gives 70n = 5 x 90 + 66(n - 5), so 70n = 450 + 66n - 330, which gives 4n = 120 and n = 30. The transferable idea: a whole-group mean is a weighted mean of the group means, so write the total in two ways and compare.
solutions.elegant: Balance about the mean: the top five are 20 points above 70 each, a surplus of 100. Each other student is 4 points below, so there are 100 / 4 = 25 of them, and the class has 25 + 5 = 30 students.

problems.whyOnTest: The balancing view makes this quick, and the trap is giving the 25 students of the second group instead of the whole class.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The three medians of a triangle meet at its centroid. A line through the centroid is drawn parallel to one side, cutting off a small triangle at the opposite corner. What fraction of the original triangle's area does the small triangle have?

choices.misconception: I put the centroid one third of the way from the opposite corner, so I used a scale of 1/3 and squared it.
I thought any line through the centre of a triangle cuts its area in half.
I worked out the area of the other piece, the strip between the line and the side.
I used the length scale of 2/3 without squaring it for area.

hints: How far from the corner is the centroid, as a fraction of a median?
The small triangle is similar to the original, so its share of the area is the square of the scale factor. The position of the centroid along a median gives that scale factor.
The centroid is two thirds of the way from a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side.

solutions.reliable: The centroid lies 2/3 of the way along each median from the corner. So the parallel line is 2/3 of the way from the corner to the opposite side, and the small triangle is a copy of the original scaled by 2/3. Areas scale by the square, so the fraction is 2/3 x 2/3 = 4/9. The transferable idea: for similar figures, find the length scale first and square it for area.

problems.whyOnTest: It combines the centroid's 2 to 1 split with area scaling, and both 2/3 and 5/9 catch a half-finished calculation.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two positive numbers have a product of 24 and a difference of 5. What is their sum?

choices.misconception: I found the two numbers, 8 and 3, and gave the smaller one instead of their sum.
I added the square of the difference to the product, 25 + 24 = 49, and took the square root.
I found the two numbers and gave the larger one instead of their sum.
I picked the factor pair 4 and 6 of 24 without checking that their difference is 5.

hints: Read the question again: what exactly is being asked for?
Either find the two numbers by testing factor pairs of 24, or use the identity that links the square of a sum, the square of a difference and the product.
The pair 8 and 3 has product 24 and difference 5.

solutions.reliable: The factor pairs of 24 are 1 and 24, 2 and 12, 3 and 8, 4 and 6, and only 3 and 8 differ by 5. Since the numbers need not be whole, check that the sum is fixed anyway: (a + b)² = (a - b)² + 4ab = 25 + 96 = 121, so a + b = 11. The transferable idea: once you have found the two numbers, stop and answer the question actually asked, here their sum.
solutions.elegant: Use (a + b)² = (a - b)² + 4ab = 25 + 96 = 121, so a + b = 11 without finding a or b at all.

problems.whyOnTest: Finding 8 and 3 feels like the finish line, but the question asks for their sum, and the choices offer both numbers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: For how many whole numbers n from 1 to 100 does 2^n + 3^n end in the digit 5?

choices.misconception: I thought that since neither 2^n nor 3^n is a multiple of 5, their sum could not be one either.
I thought the last digits repeat every 10 values of n, with only n = 1 working in each block of ten.
I thought the exponent itself had to be a multiple of 5 for the sum to end in 5.
I found that n = 1 works but missed n = 3, so I counted only n = 1, 5, 9, ..., 97.

hints: Write the last digits of 2^n and 3^n for n from 1 to 4.
Last digits of powers repeat in cycles. Both cycles here have length 4, so the last digit of the sum repeats every 4 values of n. Work out one full cycle, then count.
The last digits of 2^n run 2, 4, 8, 6 and those of 3^n run 3, 9, 7, 1.

solutions.reliable: The last digits of 2^n cycle 2, 4, 8, 6 and those of 3^n cycle 3, 9, 7, 1. Adding them: n = 1 gives 5, n = 2 gives 13, n = 3 gives 15 and n = 4 gives 7, so the sum ends in 5 exactly when n is odd. There are 50 odd numbers from 1 to 100. The transferable idea: last digits of powers repeat, so one full cycle answers the question for every n.
solutions.elegant: For odd n, a^n + b^n is divisible by a + b, so 2^n + 3^n is a multiple of 5, and it is odd, so it ends in 5. For even n = 2m, 2^n + 3^n = 4^m + 9^m, and 4^m and 9^m always leave the same remainder on division by 5, either 1 or 4, so the sum leaves 2 or 3, never 0.

problems.whyOnTest: Last-digit cycles turn a question about 100 huge numbers into a four-case check, and the distractors come from spotting only part of the pattern.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In the multiplication AB x AB = CAB, each letter stands for a digit. AB is a two-digit number and CAB is a three-digit number. What is A + B + C?

choices.misconception: I let A be 0 and used 05 x 05 = 025, even though AB must be a two-digit number.
I found AB = 25 and the product 625, then gave only the digit C instead of A + B + C.
I found AB = 25 but gave only A + B, forgetting to add C.
I chose 76, whose square 5776 also ends in 76, took C as 5 and ignored that the square has four digits.

hints: The square of AB must end in the same two digits as AB.
AB squared has only three digits, which limits how big AB can be. Its square also ends in AB, so first find which last digits B survive being squared.
B x B must end in the digit B, so B is 0, 1, 5 or 6, and AB is at most 31.

solutions.reliable: Since AB x AB is at most 999, AB is at most 31. The last digit of B x B must be B, so B is 0, 1, 5 or 6. Checking AB from 10 to 31 with those endings: 10, 11, 15, 16, 20, 21, 25, 26, 30 and 31 have squares 100, 121, 225, 256, 400, 441, 625, 676, 900 and 961. Only 625 ends in the number being squared, so A = 2, B = 5, C = 6 and A + B + C = 13. The transferable idea: in a digit puzzle, use a size bound and the last digit first, which leaves only a few cases.
solutions.elegant: AB squared ending in AB means AB x (AB - 1) is a multiple of 100. Two neighbouring numbers share no factor, so one of them is a multiple of 25 and the other a multiple of 4. Below 32 the only option is 25 and 24, so AB = 25 and the product is 625.

problems.whyOnTest: Bounding the size of AB and using the last digit cuts the search to a few checks, a standard move in digit puzzles.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many whole numbers from 1 to 100 contain the digit 7, or are divisible by 7, or both?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the numbers in both groups twice instead of once.
I counted 20 numbers containing a 7, counting 77 twice, before subtracting the overlap.
I treated 77 as the only number in both groups, forgetting 7 and 70.
I added the two counts and did not subtract the numbers that are in both groups.

hints: Count each group separately, then look for numbers in both.
This is inclusion and exclusion with two sets: add the two counts, then subtract the numbers counted twice. Careful counting of each group, and of the overlap, is the whole problem.
There are 19 numbers containing a 7, 14 multiples of 7, and the overlap is 7, 70 and 77.

solutions.reliable: Numbers containing a 7: ten end in 7 (7, 17, ..., 97) and ten lie from 70 to 79, with 77 in both lists, so there are 19. Multiples of 7 up to 100: 14. Numbers in both groups: 7, 70 and 77, so 3. The total is 19 + 14 - 3 = 30. The transferable idea: add the two groups, subtract the overlap exactly once, and list the overlap rather than guess it.

problems.whyOnTest: There are two overlaps to handle, 77 inside the digit count and three numbers shared by the groups, and each slip gives a listed distractor.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A drawer holds 3 pairs of black gloves and 2 pairs of white gloves, all mixed up. Each pair is one left glove and one right glove. In the dark, how many gloves must you take out to be certain of having a left glove and a right glove of the same colour?

choices.misconception: I treated the gloves like socks: three gloves give two of one colour, but those two could both be left gloves.
I found the largest handful with no matching left and right, which is 5, and gave that instead of one more.
I thought the worst case was drawing all 6 black gloves with no match and then needing one more, forgetting that 6 black gloves must include both hands.
I thought I might have to take every glove in the drawer to be sure.

hints: Imagine the unluckiest possible handful.
Worst-case counting: build the largest handful that still has no left and right glove of the same colour. The answer is one more than the size of that handful.
For each colour you can take every glove of one hand only, for example all 3 black left gloves and both white left gloves.

solutions.reliable: A handful with no wearable pair can hold, for each colour, gloves of only one hand. So it has at most 3 black gloves and 2 white gloves, 5 in all, for example the five left gloves. Whatever such a handful of 5 is, a sixth glove is the missing hand of its colour, so 6 gloves always contain a matching left and right. The transferable idea: the answer to a question about being certain is one more than the largest bad case.

problems.whyOnTest: The left and right condition changes the familiar sock answer, so the question tests building the true worst case rather than reusing a formula.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A dog is tied by a 6 m rope to one corner of a square shed with sides of 4 m. The dog stays outside the shed, and the rope cannot pass through the shed. What is the area of the ground the dog can reach?

choices.misconception: I thought the shed blocks three quarters of the circle, leaving only a quarter circle of radius 6.
I thought the shed blocks half of the circle, leaving a semicircle of radius 6.
I took three quarters of the circle of radius 6 but forgot that the rope can bend round the corners of the shed.
I let the rope bend round the corner on one side of the shed but forgot the other side.

hints: Draw the shed and sweep the rope all the way round it.
Away from the shed the dog sweeps most of a circle. When the rope lies along a side, it wraps round the next corner, and the rope left over sweeps a smaller quarter circle. Add the pieces.
Three quarters of a circle of radius 6, plus a quarter circle of radius 2 beyond each of the two neighbouring corners.

solutions.reliable: The shed blocks one quarter of the directions from its corner, so the dog sweeps three quarters of a circle of radius 6, with area 3/4 x 36π = 27π. When the rope lies along a side of the shed, 6 - 4 = 2 m is left, and swinging round the next corner it sweeps a quarter circle of radius 2, with area π. This happens at both neighbouring corners, adding 2π, and the two small pieces lie on different sides of the shed, so they do not overlap. The total is 27π + 2π = 29π m². The transferable idea: draw the diagram and follow the rope, because each corner it wraps round starts a new, smaller arc.

problems.whyOnTest: Drawing the shed and the rope reveals the small quarter circles round the corners, which every distractor misses or miscounts.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana claims: 'If a and b are both odd whole numbers, then a² + b² is never a perfect square.' Which of these is correct?

choices.text: Ana is right, because a² + b² is always 2 more than a multiple of 4, and no perfect square is.

choices.misconception: I used the 3, 4, 5 triangle without noticing that 4 is even.

choices.text: Ana is right, because a² + b² is always even, and no perfect square is even.
choices.misconception: I forgot that even numbers such as 4, 16 and 36 are perfect squares.

choices.text: Ana is right, but only for small numbers; larger odd numbers might break the rule.
choices.misconception: I thought checking examples was the only way to know, so I assumed big numbers might still break the rule.
I remembered the 7, 24, 25 triangle and did not check that 24 is even.

hints: What remainder does an odd square leave when divided by 4?
Suppose a² + b² were a perfect square and look for a contradiction. Remainders on division by 4 are the right tool, because every square leaves remainder 0 or 1.
An odd number can be written 2k + 1, and its square is 4k² + 4k + 1.

solutions.reliable: An odd number is 2k + 1 for some whole number k, and (2k + 1)² = 4(k² + k) + 1, so every odd square leaves remainder 1 on division by 4. Then a² + b² leaves remainder 2. An even square (2m)² = 4m² leaves remainder 0 and an odd square leaves 1, so no perfect square leaves remainder 2. Ana is right. The transferable idea: to show a number is never a square, find a remainder that squares cannot have.

problems.whyOnTest: Remainders on division by 4 prove a claim about infinitely many numbers, and the famous right-angled triangles tempt anyone who skips the word odd.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two cars each drive 240 km. Car P drives the first half of the distance at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Car Q drives at 40 km/h for the first half of its travel time and at 60 km/h for the second half. They start together. How many minutes before P does Q arrive?

choices.misconception: I thought both cars average 50 km/h, because 50 is halfway between 40 and 60.
I found the gap as 0.2 hours and read it as 20 minutes.
I gave car P's average speed, 48 km/h, instead of the difference in time.
I thought car Q takes 240 / 60 = 4 hours, as if it drove at 60 km/h all the way, so the gap came out as 1 hour.

hints: Work out each car's total time separately.
Equal times at two speeds give the simple average speed, but equal distances do not, because the car spends longer at the slower speed. Compute each car's total time directly.
Car P takes 120/40 + 120/60 hours. Car Q averages 50 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Car P: 120 km at 40 km/h takes 3 hours and 120 km at 60 km/h takes 2 hours, so 5 hours in all. Car Q spends equal times at 40 and 60 km/h, so its average speed is 50 km/h and it takes 240 / 50 = 4.8 hours. The difference is 0.2 hours, which is 0.2 x 60 = 12 minutes. The transferable idea: average speed is total distance over total time, and it equals the simple average of two speeds only when the times are equal.

problems.whyOnTest: Averaging the two speeds works for car Q but not for car P, and the question probes exactly that difference, plus a decimal-hours trap.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Nine different positive whole numbers add up to 60. What is the largest possible value of their median, the middle number when they are listed in order?

choices.misconception: I thought the median could not be bigger than the mean, 60/9, and rounded down.
I let the four numbers below the median all be 1, forgetting they must be different.
I let the four numbers above the median all equal the median, forgetting they must be bigger and different.
I forgot that all nine numbers must be different and made the others as small as possible anyway.

hints: To push the median up, make the other numbers as small as the rules allow.

Extremal thinking: the four numbers below the median should be as small as possible, and so should the four above it, while still being bigger than the median and all different. This gives an inequality for the median.
With median m, the sum is at least 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + m + (m + 1) + (m + 2) + (m + 3) + (m + 4).

solutions.reliable: List the numbers in order with median m. The four below it are at least 1, 2, 3 and 4, and the four above are at least m + 1, m + 2, m + 3 and m + 4. So 60 is at least 10 + 5m + 10, which gives 5m at most 40 and m at most 8. For m = 8, the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 are different and add to 60. The answer is 8. The transferable idea: to make one value as large as possible, make everything else as small as the conditions allow, then show the bound is reached.

problems.whyOnTest: The bound uses every condition at once, and each distractor drops exactly one of them: difference below, difference above, or the link to the mean.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Seven points are equally spaced around a circle. Each point is joined to the two points that are three places away from it around the circle, making the sharp seven-pointed star shown. What is the sum of the seven angles at the tips of the star?

figure.alt: Seven points equally spaced on a dashed circle. Each point is joined by straight lines to the two points three places away around the circle, forming a seven-pointed star with very narrow tips at the seven points.

choices.misconception: I thought that walking round the star turns through one full turn, so the tip angles must add to 360°.
I worked with the blunter star made by joining points two places apart, whose tips add to 540°.
I used the angle sum of a seven-sided polygon instead of the angles at the star's tips.
I treated each tip as the corner of its own triangle and added 180° for each of the seven tips.

hints: Each tip is an angle whose corner lies on the circle.
An angle with its corner on a circle is half of the arc it cuts off on the far side. Work out which arc each tip angle stands on, in terms of the seven equal arcs between the points.
The seven points split the circle into seven equal arcs. Each tip angle stands on just one of those arcs.

solutions.reliable: The seven points divide the circle into seven equal arcs of 360°/7. The tip at any point is joined to the two points three places away on either side, and those two points are neighbours, so the tip angle stands on a single small arc. An angle with its corner on the circle is half of its arc, so each tip is 180°/7, and the seven tips add up to 180°. The transferable idea: angles with their corner on a circle are measured by the arcs they cut off.
solutions.elegant: The seven tips stand on the seven different small arcs, which together make the whole circle of 360°. Each tip is half of its arc, so all the tips together make half of 360°, which is 180°.

problems.whyOnTest: Seeing the tips as angles standing on arcs makes a star with no obvious triangles easy, while polygon angle-sum habits lead to the distractors.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Six teams play a tournament in which every team plays every other team once. A win earns 3 points, a draw earns 1 point for each team, and a loss earns 0. At the end, one team has strictly fewer points than every other team. What is the largest number of points that team can have?

choices.misconception: I assumed the points always total 30, as if every game were drawn, and solved 6x + 5 at most 30.
I imagined every game being drawn, so every team has 5, and took that as the most the bottom team could have.
I divided the largest possible total, 45, by 6 and rounded 7.5 down, forgetting the other teams need more.
I divided the largest possible total, 45, by 6 and rounded 7.5 up.

hints: What is the largest possible total of all the teams' points?

If the bottom team has x points, each other team has at least x + 1. Compare that smallest possible total with the largest total a tournament can produce, then build a results table that reaches the bound.
There are 15 games, and each one gives out at most 3 points, so the total is at most 45.

solutions.reliable: There are 15 games, and each gives out 3 points if won or 2 if drawn, so the total is at most 45. If the bottom team has x points and the other five at least x + 1 each, the total is at least 6x + 5, so 6x + 5 is at most 45 and x is at most 6. Six is possible. Call the teams A to F. A beats B and C and loses to D, E and F, so A has 6. B beats C and D, draws with E and loses to F, so B has 7. C beats D and E and draws with F, so C has 7. D beats A, E and F, so D has 9. E beats A and F and draws with B, so E has 7. F beats A and B and draws with C, so F has 7. A is strictly last with 6. The transferable idea: bound the answer using a total, then build an example to show the bound is reached.

problems.whyOnTest: It needs both halves of an extremal argument, a bound from the total and an example that meets it, and each distractor skips one half.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In a coordinate plane, a bee flies in straight lines from P(2, 3) to a point on the y-axis, then to a point on the x-axis, and then to Q(5, 1). What is the shortest possible total length of its flight?

choices.misconception: I measured straight from P to Q, forgetting that the bee must visit both axes.
I reflected Q in the x-axis but forgot that the bee must touch the y-axis too.
I reflected P in the y-axis but forgot that the bee must touch the x-axis too.
I thought the best plan was to touch both axes at once by flying through the origin.

hints: Reflections can turn a bent path into a straight one.
Reflect P in the y-axis and Q in the x-axis. Each leg that touches an axis then matches a leg to a reflected point, and the shortest route between two points is a straight segment.
The reflected points are (-2, 3) and (5, -1).

solutions.reliable: Reflect P in the y-axis to P'(-2, 3) and Q in the x-axis to Q'(5, -1). The leg from P to a point on the y-axis has the same length as the leg from P' to that point, and the leg from a point on the x-axis to Q has the same length as the leg to Q'. So every flight is at least as long as the straight segment P'Q', which is √(7² + 4²) = √65. That segment crosses the y-axis at (0, 13/7) and then the x-axis at (13/4, 0), so the bee can fly exactly this route, and the shortest flight is √65. The transferable idea: each forced touch of a line is handled by a reflection, which straightens a broken path.
solutions.elegant: Reflecting P in the y-axis and then in the x-axis sends it to (-2, -3), and the distance from there to Q(5, 1) is √(49 + 16) = √65.

problems.whyOnTest: Two reflections straighten the path, and each distractor comes from reflecting only once or from a natural but wrong guess about where to touch.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Lines parallel to the sides cut an equilateral triangle of side 4 into 16 small equilateral triangles of side 1. A beetle walks from small triangle to small triangle, each step crossing a shared side, and never enters a small triangle twice. What is the largest number of small triangles it can visit, including its starting one?

choices.misconception: I made the beetle walk along just the bottom row, which has 7 small triangles.
I saw that the route alternates between upward and downward triangles but did not let it start and finish on upward ones.
I noticed only that the three corner triangles, each with a single neighbour, cannot all be visited, and left out just one.
I thought a clever enough route could visit every small triangle.

hints: Small triangles point either up or down. Which kinds can be neighbours?
Use a colouring argument: every step goes between an upward and a downward triangle, so the route alternates. Count each kind, and the smaller count limits the length of the route.
There are 10 upward small triangles and only 6 downward ones.

solutions.reliable: The rows of small triangles contain 1, 3, 5 and 7 triangles, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 point up and 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 point down. Two small triangles sharing a side always point in opposite directions, so the route alternates up, down, up, down. With only 6 downward triangles available, the route has at most 6 downward and 7 upward triangles, so at most 13 in all. Thirteen is possible: start in the bottom left corner and walk right through 6 triangles of the bottom row, step up and walk left through 4 triangles, step up and walk right through 2, then step into the top triangle. The transferable idea: when every move switches between two kinds of cell, the scarcer kind limits the route.

problems.whyOnTest: Sorting the triangles into up and down turns a fiddly search into a one-line bound, while trial routes suggest misleading answers.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A convex hexagon is drawn so that no three of its diagonals meet at the same point inside it. All of its diagonals are drawn. Into how many regions do they divide the hexagon?

choices.misconception: I thought each diagonal adds just one region, giving 1 + 9, and ignored the crossings.
I added one region for each crossing point but forgot the regions added by the diagonals themselves.
I found 1, 4 and 11 regions for a triangle, a quadrilateral and a pentagon, saw gaps of 3 and 7, and guessed the next gap was 11.
I drew a regular hexagon, where the three long diagonals all meet at the centre, and counted its regions, which is one fewer.

hints: Try the quadrilateral and the pentagon first.
Small cases show what each new diagonal adds: one region for the diagonal itself, plus one more for every diagonal it crosses. So count the diagonals and the crossing points.
A hexagon has 9 diagonals. Every choice of 4 of the 6 corners gives exactly one crossing point, so there are 15 crossings.

solutions.reliable: Start with 1 region. Drawing a diagonal adds 1 region, plus 1 more for every earlier diagonal it crosses, so the number of regions is 1 + (number of diagonals) + (number of crossings). A hexagon has 6 x 3 / 2 = 9 diagonals. Each crossing comes from exactly one choice of 4 corners, whose two diagonals cross once, and there are 15 ways to choose 4 of the 6 corners. So there are 1 + 9 + 15 = 25 regions. The rule checks against small cases: a quadrilateral gives 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 and a pentagon 1 + 5 + 5 = 11. The transferable idea: use small cases to find what each new line contributes, then count those contributions directly.

problems.whyOnTest: Small cases reveal the rule of 1 plus diagonals plus crossings, and guessing from a short list of numbers instead of from the reason gives 22.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: In how many ways can 3 numbers be chosen from 1, 2, 3, ..., 10 so that no two of the chosen numbers are consecutive?

choices.misconception: I subtracted every choice containing a consecutive pair, 9 pairs times 8 third numbers, from 120, not noticing that runs like 4, 5, 6 were subtracted twice.
I squeezed out only one gap instead of two, and counted choices of 3 from 9 numbers.
I removed only the choices of three numbers in a row, such as 4, 5, 6.
I counted all choices of 3 numbers and ignored the condition.

hints: Picture the gaps that must sit between the chosen numbers.
Close up the forced gaps: taking away 0, 1 and 2 from the chosen numbers in increasing order turns every allowed choice into an ordinary choice from a smaller set, and the step can be undone.
If a < b < c have gaps between them, then a, b - 1 and c - 2 are three different numbers from 1 to 8.

solutions.reliable: Count all choices and subtract the bad ones. There are 10 x 9 x 8 / 6 = 120 choices in all. A choice is bad if it contains a consecutive pair. There are 9 consecutive pairs, each with 8 possible third numbers, giving 72, but the 8 runs of three in a row, such as 4, 5, 6, contain two pairs and were counted twice. So there are 72 - 8 = 64 bad choices and 120 - 64 = 56 good ones. The transferable idea: when subtracting bad cases, check whether any of them was removed twice.
solutions.elegant: Write a choice as a < b < c with gaps of at least 2 and send it to a, b - 1, c - 2. This gives any three different numbers from 1 to 8, and each such triple comes back to exactly one valid choice, so the count is 8 x 7 x 6 / 6 = 56.

problems.whyOnTest: The direct subtraction hides an overlap trap and the gap-closing trick avoids it, so the problem rewards either care or insight.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Counters are placed on some squares of a 7 by 7 board so that no two counters are on squares that touch, not even at a corner. What is the largest number of counters that can be placed?

choices.misconception: I split the board into 2 by 2 blocks, put one counter in each of the 9 full blocks and ignored the strips left over at the edges.
I used rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 but put only 3 counters in each, starting from the second square.
I divided the 49 squares by 4, since each counter seems to need a 2 by 2 space, and rounded up.
I put a counter on every square of one colour of a chessboard pattern, forgetting that diagonal neighbours touch at a corner.

hints: Try putting counters on every other square of every other row.
For the upper bound, cut the board into pieces in which every two squares touch, so each piece holds at most one counter. Then find an arrangement with a counter in every piece.
Group the rows as 2, 2, 2 and 1, and the columns the same way. That cuts the board into 16 pieces.
