problems.statement: You have a two-pan balance and four weights of 1 g, 3 g, 9 g and 27 g. Any weights may go on either pan, next to the object or opposite it. How many different whole-number masses, starting from 1 g, can be measured exactly in a single weighing?

choices.misconception: I put weights only on the pan opposite the object, so I counted only the sums of the weights.
I counted every way of placing each weight on the left, on the right or off the balance.
I counted every placement except all weights off, without noticing each mass is reached by two mirror-image placements.
I counted zero as one of the masses, as if weighing nothing counted.

hints: A weight next to the object counts as a negative.

Each weight can be added, subtracted or left out, so the measured mass is a sum of plus or minus the weights. Find the largest mass possible and ask whether every whole number below it can be reached.
The largest mass is 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40. Check that small cases such as 2 = 3 - 1 and 5 = 9 - 3 - 1 work.

solutions.reliable: A weight opposite the object adds its mass and one beside the object subtracts it, so the object's mass is a sum where each of 1, 3, 9, 27 appears with +, - or not at all. The largest is 40. Every value from 1 to 40 can be made: 1, 3 - 1, 3, 3 + 1, 9 - 3 - 1, and so on, since with 1 and 3 you reach every mass from 1 to 4, adding 9 extends this to every mass up to 13, and adding 27 extends it to 40. So 40 masses. The transferable idea: when each item can be used positively, negatively or not at all, powers of 3 cover every whole number up to their total.
solutions.elegant: There are 3 to the power 4 = 81 placements. One gives 0, and the other 80 split into mirror pairs giving m and -m, so at most 40 positive masses, and since every value from 1 to 40 is reached, the answer is 40. The transferable idea: count placements, then divide out the symmetry.

problems.whyOnTest: Balance puzzles test whether you allow weights on both pans, which turns a doubling count into a powers-of-three count.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ten different positive whole numbers add up to 75. What is the largest value the biggest of them can have?

choices.misconception: I made the other nine numbers all equal to 1, forgetting the numbers must be different.
I let the nine smaller numbers be 0 to 8, but 0 is not a positive number.
I subtracted 1 + 2 + ... + 10 from 75, which wrongly includes a tenth small number.
I found the smallest the biggest number can be, not the largest.

hints: To make one number big, make the rest small.
The biggest number is largest when the other nine take up as little of the total as possible. Find the smallest possible sum of nine different positive whole numbers.
The nine smallest different positive whole numbers are 1 to 9, which add to 45.

solutions.reliable: The other nine numbers are different positive whole numbers, so their sum is at least 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45. Then the biggest is at most 75 - 45 = 30, and 1, 2, ..., 9, 30 shows that 30 is reached. The transferable idea: to push one quantity to an extreme, push everything else to the opposite extreme, then check the extreme case is allowed.

problems.whyOnTest: Extremal questions reward pushing every other quantity to its limit, and the trap is breaking one of the stated conditions while doing it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Ana and Ben together can paint a fence in 12 days, Ben and Cai together in 15 days, and Ana and Cai together in 20 days. Each person always works at the same steady speed. How many days would Ana need to paint the fence alone?

choices.misconception: I found how long all three would take working together and stopped there.
I forgot to halve the sum of the three pair rates before subtracting Ben and Cai's rate.
I added and subtracted the times, 12 + 20 - 15, as if times combined like rates.
I assumed Ana alone takes twice as long as Ana and Ben together.

hints: Work with fractions of the fence per day, not with days.
Turn each pair's time into a rate. Adding all three pair rates counts each person's rate twice, which tells you the rate of all three together. Then remove the pair that does not include Ana.
Per day: Ana + Ben = 1/12, Ben + Cai = 1/15, Ana + Cai = 1/20. These add to 1/5, which is twice the rate of all three.

solutions.reliable: As fractions of the fence per day, the three pair rates add to 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 5/60 + 4/60 + 3/60 = 1/5. That counts everyone twice, so all three together paint 1/10 per day. Ben and Cai paint 1/15 per day, so Ana alone paints 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30 per day and needs 30 days. The transferable idea: in work problems, rates add and times do not.
solutions.elegant: Take 60 days as a convenient length: in 60 days the pairs would paint 5, 4 and 3 fences, so all three together paint 6 fences, of which Ben and Cai paint 4, leaving 2 fences in 60 days for Ana. The transferable idea: choose a common time to turn rates into whole numbers.

problems.whyOnTest: Combined work questions test whether you convert times into rates, and the symmetric pair data hides a neat 'count everyone twice' step.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: I think of a number. I double it, add 6, then halve the result. The answer is 5 less than three times my number. What number did I think of?

choices.misconception: I halved only the 6, writing 2x + 3, instead of halving the whole of 2x + 6.
I forgot to halve at all, and set 2x + 6 equal to 3x - 5.
I found the final answer of the steps, not the number I started with.
I read '5 less than three times my number' as 5 - 3x.

hints: Call the number x and follow the steps exactly.
Turn each instruction into algebra in order, using brackets so that 'halve the result' acts on everything so far. Then write the second sentence as an expression and set the two equal.
The steps give (2x + 6) / 2 = x + 3, and '5 less than three times my number' is 3x - 5.

solutions.reliable: Doubling and adding 6 gives 2x + 6, and halving that gives x + 3. Setting x + 3 = 3x - 5 gives 2x = 8, so x = 4. Check: 4 doubled is 8, plus 6 is 14, halved is 7, and three times 4 minus 5 is also 7. The transferable idea: translate a sentence step by step, with brackets around 'the result' so each operation acts on everything before it.

problems.whyOnTest: Turning a chain of instructions into an equation is a basic skill, and the wrong choices come from the small translation slips everyone makes.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three friends choose seats in a row of 7 empty chairs so that no two of them sit next to each other. In how many different ways can they do this, if it matters who sits where?

choices.misconception: I counted which three chairs are used but forgot the three friends can swap among those chairs.
I counted all seatings of three people in 7 chairs and ignored the rule about sitting next to each other.
I counted sets of three chairs without the rule and without arranging the friends.
I only removed the seatings where all three sit together, not those where just two are side by side.

hints: First decide which chairs are used, then who sits where.
Choose the set of chairs first, keeping gaps between them, and only afterwards place the three friends. A neat way to count gapped chairs is to remove the compulsory empty chairs between friends.
Between the friends there must be at least one empty chair in each of the two gaps. Take those 2 chairs away and choose any 3 of the remaining 5.

solutions.reliable: Listing the chair sets with gaps, written as chair numbers: 135, 136, 137, 146, 147, 157, 246, 247, 257, 357 gives 10 sets. In each set the three friends can be arranged in 3 times 2 times 1 = 6 ways, so there are 60 seatings. The transferable idea: in restricted counting, choose the positions under the rule first and arrange the people afterwards.
solutions.elegant: Remove one empty chair from each of the two gaps that must exist; any choice of 3 of the remaining 5 chairs then corresponds to exactly one gapped choice in the original row, so there are 10 chair sets and 10 times 6 = 60 seatings. The transferable idea: squeeze out the forced gaps to turn a restricted count into an unrestricted one.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting with a 'not next to each other' rule tests whether you separate choosing places from arranging people and handle every forbidden case.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The eight corners of a regular octagon are marked. How many triangles with all three corners at marked points have a right angle?

choices.misconception: I counted third corners on only one side of each of the 4 longest diagonals.
I only counted the right triangles whose two shorter sides are equal.
I counted every triangle with corners at the marked points without checking for a right angle.
I counted each right triangle twice, once from each end of its longest side.

hints: All eight corners lie on one circle.

A triangle drawn inside a circle with its corners on the circle has a right angle exactly when one of its sides is a diameter. Count the diameters that join two corners, then count the possible third corners for each.
The octagon has 4 diameters joining opposite corners, and each one can be completed with any of the other 6 corners.

solutions.reliable: The corners of a regular octagon lie on a circle. A triangle with its corners on a circle has a right angle exactly when one side is a diameter, and the right angle is then at the third corner. The diameters joining two corners are the 4 lines through opposite corners. Each can be completed by any of the remaining 6 corners, and a right triangle has only one longest side, so no triangle is counted twice. That gives 4 times 6 = 24. The transferable idea: when shapes are hidden among points on a circle, a right angle means a diameter.

problems.whyOnTest: Counting hidden shapes is about finding the feature that pins each one down, here the diameter that every right triangle in a circle must use.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The diagonals of the quadrilateral ABCD are perpendicular. AB = 5, BC = 6 and CD = 7. What is the length of DA?

choices.misconception: I guessed the sides keep going up by one, 5, 6, 7 and then 8.
I set AB squared plus BC squared equal to CD squared plus DA squared, pairing neighbouring sides instead of opposite ones.
I set AB squared plus DA squared equal to BC squared plus CD squared, pairing the two sides at A against the two sides at C.
I added the squares of all three given sides, as if DA were the long side of a right triangle made from them.

hints: Call the point where the diagonals cross O.

The perpendicular diagonals cut the quadrilateral into four right triangles meeting at O. Write each side squared using Pythagoras with the two pieces of diagonal next to it, and look for a combination of sides in which every piece cancels.
AB squared = OA squared + OB squared, and likewise for the other three sides. Compare AB squared + CD squared with BC squared + DA squared.

solutions.reliable: Let the diagonals meet at O. By Pythagoras in the four right triangles at O: AB squared = OA squared + OB squared, BC squared = OB squared + OC squared, CD squared = OC squared + OD squared and DA squared = OD squared + OA squared. So AB squared + CD squared and BC squared + DA squared both equal OA squared + OB squared + OC squared + OD squared. Then 25 + 49 = 36 + DA squared, so DA squared = 38 and DA = √38. Such a quadrilateral exists, for example with OA = 4, OB = 3, OC = √27 and OD = √22. The transferable idea: when a figure splits into right triangles around one point, add the Pythagoras equations so the unknown pieces cancel.

problems.whyOnTest: Properties of quadrilaterals often hide one clean relation, and perpendicular diagonals give the sums of squares of opposite sides being equal, even though the quadrilateral itself is not fixed.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the value of 2025 times 2025 minus 2024 times 2026?

choices.misconception: I assumed 2024 times 2026 is the same as 2025 times 2025 because the two factors balance out around 2025.
I thought (n - 1)(n + 1) equals n squared minus 2, taking 1 off for each factor.
I thought (n - 1)(n + 1) equals n squared plus 1, so I got the sign of the difference backwards.
I mixed this up with 2025 squared minus 2024 squared, which is 2025 + 2024.

hints: Do not multiply out the big numbers.
Write 2024 and 2026 as 2025 minus 1 and 2025 plus 1. There is a standard product for (n - 1)(n + 1) that makes the subtraction collapse.
With n = 2025, (n - 1)(n + 1) = n squared - 1, so the expression is n squared - (n squared - 1).

solutions.reliable: Let n = 2025. Then 2024 times 2026 = (n - 1)(n + 1) = n squared - 1, so the expression is n squared - (n squared - 1) = 1. A small check: 3 times 3 - 2 times 4 = 9 - 8 = 1. The transferable idea: big numbers that sit symmetrically around a centre usually call for the difference of squares, not long multiplication.
solutions.elegant: Try the same pattern with small numbers: 5 times 5 - 4 times 6 = 1 and 10 times 10 - 9 times 11 = 1. The pattern is always 1. The transferable idea: test a tiny version of an expression to spot the trick before grinding.

problems.whyOnTest: Kangaroo loves expressions that look like heavy arithmetic but collapse with one identity: spotting that is the skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A train leaves at 10:40 and arrives at 13:15. A second train leaves 25 minutes after the first and its journey takes 20 minutes less. At what time does the second train arrive?

choices.misconception: I took 20 minutes off the arrival time and forgot that the second train also leaves later.
I added the 25-minute later start and forgot that the second journey is shorter.
I worked out how long the second journey takes, not when the train arrives.
I moved the times the wrong way, taking off the 25 minutes and adding the 20.

hints: The question asks for a time of day, not a duration.
Track the two changes separately: a later start pushes the arrival later, and a shorter journey pulls it earlier. Combine them, then check that your answer is the kind of quantity being asked for.
Leaving 25 minutes later and travelling 20 minutes less means arriving 25 - 20 = 5 minutes later than the first train.

solutions.reliable: The first journey lasts from 10:40 to 13:15, which is 2 h 35 min. The second train leaves at 11:05 and takes 2 h 15 min, so it arrives at 13:20. The transferable idea: before bubbling, check that your answer is the quantity asked for, a time of day here and not a length of time.
solutions.elegant: Leaving 25 minutes later pushes the arrival 25 minutes later, and a 20-minute shorter trip brings it back 20 minutes, a net 5 minutes later than 13:15: 13:20. The transferable idea: track changes, not totals.

problems.whyOnTest: Many points are lost by answering a nearby question: here the journey length is on offer next to the arrival time the question wants.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi
